title: Benchmarking Loss Functions for Electrocardiogram Reconstruction
text: Preface & Executive Summary

title: Benchmarking Loss Functions for Electrocardiogram Reconstruction
text:
Motivation & Clinical Context
Electrocardiogram (ECG) reconstruction aims to estimate a complete 12-lead ECG representation from a reduced subset of leads—such as a single wearable-like Lead I or a 3-lead input. Mean Squared Error (MSE) is a standard objective, but conditional averaging can attenuate morphology when the missing signal is not uniquely determined by the observed leads. This handbook tests that concern rather than assuming it.

The Regression-to-the-Mean Failure (Presacan et al., 2025)
In Communications Medicine (Nature Portfolio), Presacan et al. (2025) reported regression-to-the-mean behavior in ECG reconstruction trained with MSE. More generally, squared-error population risk targets a conditional expectation; when multiple missing-lead morphologies are compatible with the observed leads, averaging can attenuate uncommon amplitudes or shapes. Whether that occurs for a particular checkpoint and endpoint is measured here rather than assumed from the theorem or prior paper.
Potential failure modes include P/T delineation error, ST-segment attenuation, and QT/QTc drift. These are hypotheses requiring artifact-backed evaluation; the book does not infer patient harm from synthetic waveforms or global similarity metrics.
       MSE Loss (Regression to Mean)          Combinatorial Composite Loss (Ours)
    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐      ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Flat P-waves / Flattened ST    │      │  Candidate shape preservation  │
    │  Damped Peak Amplitudes         │  vs  │  QTc/VCG metrics require audit │
    │  Metrics requiring audit        │      │  No assumed clinical benefit   │
    └─────────────────────────────────┘      └─────────────────────────────────┘

title: Benchmarking Loss Functions for Electrocardiogram Reconstruction
text:
How to read this handbook
For current experiment status, start with the Live Experiment Observatory, then open either the three-lead queue and source monitor or the one-lead active/pending monitor. Completed one-lead screening, spatial, convergence, and external RDB results now have separate chapters, as do completed three-lead LUDB/RDB morphology, representation, and LUDB semi-supervised delineation studies. For a visual cross-experiment view, use the Deep ECG-AIM Evidence Dashboard, which shows matched mechanism effects, learning trajectories, external transport, boundary-specific failures, and paired linear-probe intervals without merging incompatible endpoints.
The book begins with evidence, not demonstrations. The opening real-data EDA audits PTB-XL and EchoNext in depth and now provides separate, stability-audited waveform UMAPs for every locally supported clinical cohort: PTB-XL, EchoNext, LUDB, ISP, Sunnybrook, Zhejiang, and RDB. The multi-dataset atlas establishes what the smaller morphology cohorts contribute, followed by a separate Zhejiang file-level audit. Only after those measurement contracts are visible does the PTB-XL preprocessing contract explain the content-pinned tensors and lead mapping.
The remaining parts follow the causal order of the study:

Data, cohorts, and measurement — what was observed, how records were partitioned, and which claims each dataset can support.
Reconstruction models and objectives — the architectures and loss terms applied to those inputs.
Clinical and statistical evaluation — paired morphology, delineation, agreement, fairness, robustness, and uncertainty.
Benchmark and external validation — the locked 48-cell evidence, coverage-limited seven-mask generations, completed external morphology, device transfer, and EchoNext classifier preservation.

This order is deliberate. A model ranking is uninterpretable until the reader knows the units, split boundary, repeated-patient structure, endpoint prevalence, and downstream measurement contract. Synthetic examples remain in the book as executable tutorials, but they are labeled as demonstrations and never substitute for cohort evidence.

title: 1  Live Experiment Observatory
text:
1.4 Visualization contract
The live chapters deliberately distinguish three objects:

Raw metric views show observed values and remain the source of rankings.
Matched deltas compare a configuration against its registered baseline only when seed and observed lead agree.
Performance UMAP embeds standardized outcome vectors. Proximity means similar measured performance profiles; it does not establish similar encoder representations, physiology, or causal mechanisms.

title: 2  Three-Lead Active and Partial Experiment Monitor
text:
2.1 Input and evidence contract
This monitor covers the three-lead I+II+V2 reconstruction program. It does not pool one-lead ECG-AIM runs. Queue completion, checkpoint registration, storage verification, evaluation compatibility, waveform metrics, and clinical metrics are distinct states; success at one stage does not imply success at another.

4.1 Evidence contract
This chapter freezes the interpretation of the completed three-epoch 1110000, seed-42 screening experiment. It is separate from the live queue, longer convergence extensions, spatial experiments, and external RDB evaluation. A completed screening row is not a replicated confirmatory result.
The primary registered chain is A0 raw → A0 + wavelet → A0 + wavelet + SSL. E1 is a complementarity test, not an improved baseline. Lead I and lead II are separate input contracts and are never averaged before showing their individual results.

section: 4.7 What the registered contrasts actually show
text:
4.7 What the registered contrasts actually show
The wavelet increment is the clearest short-screen effect. Relative to A0 raw, the wavelet branch without SSL increases wave mIoU by 0.079 on lead I and 0.043 on lead II, boundary F1 by 0.060 and 0.016, and P-wave IoU by 0.171 and 0.083. QRS IoU changes by only 0.001–0.003. This concentration on P/T rather than QRS is mechanistically plausible, but it is still an internal three-epoch result. The branch costs approximately 4.16 GB additional peak GPU memory.
The SSL increment is heterogeneous. On lead I it changes mean Pearson by −0.0005, lower-tail Pearson by −0.0041, and boundary F1 by −0.0011. On lead II it changes those endpoints by +0.0030, +0.0040, and +0.0358. It also adds about 8.45 GB beyond the wavelet-only model. The correct screen-level conclusion is therefore possible lead-II delineation complementarity, not a general SSL improvement.
Replacing Morlet phase with UEG phase changes mean Pearson by less than 0.0002 on either lead. Boundary F1 increases by 0.0030 on lead I and 0.0105 on lead II, but the lower-tail Pearson direction reverses between leads. This is too small and inconsistent for a physiology claim without longer matched training.
Only the lead-II E1 complementarity cell completed. It is essentially tied with A0+wavelet+SSL while using approximately 5.94 GB more memory. Because lead I is missing, this contrast is both single-seed and asymmetrically censored.

Mean Pearson and reconstruction loss are almost redundant in rank (absolute Spearman approximately 0.99), while boundary F1 correlates only about 0.11 with mean Pearson. Wave mIoU is moderately coupled to both. This explains why a reconstruction leader need not be a boundary leader and why a single composite score embeds a scientific value judgement.
With 115 completed rows and many endpoints, the metric-wise maximum is strongly subject to winner’s curse. A configuration appearing once at the top is a candidate, not a confirmed effect. The registered contrasts above are more interpretable than post-hoc leaderboard mining, even though they still lack replication.

text:
4.9 Metric-Space Screening UMAP Manifolds
To map the high-dimensional performance landscape across all 115 completed screening configurations, we compute 2D and 3D non-linear UMAP manifolds over the standardized matrix of all available validation, delineation, loss, and hardware metrics:


Code
import umap
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import plotly.graph_objects as go

valid_screen_metrics = [m for m in metrics if completed[m].notna().sum() > 80 and completed[m].std() > 1e-6]
X_screen = completed[valid_screen_metrics].fillna(completed[valid_screen_metrics].median()).values
X_screen_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_screen)

reducer_screen_2d = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=10, min_dist=0.2, random_state=42)
u_screen_2d = reducer_screen_2d.fit_transform(X_screen_scaled)
completed["UMAP1"] = u_screen_2d[:, 0]
completed["UMAP2"] = u_screen_2d[:, 1]

fig_screen_umap2d = px.scatter(
    completed, x="UMAP1", y="UMAP2",
    color="observed_lead", symbol="cell_name",
    size="metric.miou_wave", hover_name="id",
    hover_data=["cell_name", "metric.val_missing_pearson", "metric.boundary_f1_smoke", "metric.P_iou", "metric.T_iou"],
    labels={"UMAP1": "Screening Metric UMAP 1", "UMAP2": "Screening Metric UMAP 2",
            "observed_lead": "Observed Lead", "cell_name": "Cell Name"},
    title="2D Metric-Space UMAP: Global Topological Clustering Across All 115 Screening Models"
)
fig_screen_umap2d.update_layout(height=620)
fig_screen_umap2d.show()

reducer_screen_3d = umap.UMAP(n_components=3, n_neighbors=10, min_dist=0.2, random_state=42)
u_screen_3d = reducer_screen_3d.fit_transform(X_screen_scaled)
completed["UMAP3D_1"] = u_screen_3d[:, 0]

fig_screen_umap3d = px.scatter_3d(

text:
5.1 Experiment identity and architectural taxonomy
This completed study investigated ten distinct architectural and spatial conditioning strategies crossed with three factorial masks (1000000, 1010010, 1110000) and two observed leads (Lead I and Lead II), generating 60 completed training runs.
The ten architectural variants represent four distinct conceptual paradigms:
crumbs: 5  Completed One-Lead ECG-AIM Spatial Study

title: 5  Completed One-Lead ECG-AIM Spatial Study
text:
Unconditioned Baselines: a0 (Standard 1-lead UNet baseline without lead coordinates).
Coordinate & Angular Conditioning:

b1_panorama: Cylindrical panorama coordinate projection.
c1_panorama_hybrid: Hybrid coordinate embedding and feature concatenation.
d1_panorama_relative: Relative pairwise inter-lead angular displacement.
t000_exact_theta: 2D trigonometric angle encoding (\cos \theta, \sin \theta).
t111_exact_theta: Full 3D trigonometric orientation vectors.

Advanced Modulation:

e1_panorama_film: True spherical/cylindrical geometry with Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM).
pa1_panorama_author: Author baseline spatial fusion formulation.

Falsification & Capacity Controls:

cm1_capacity_matched: Parameter-matched control (identical parameter count to spatial variants but without anatomical coordinates).
pg1_permuted_geometry: Scrambled anatomical lead coordinates (tests whether physiological correctness matters).

5.6.1 Statistical Evaluation:

E_1 vs Permuted Geometry (PG_1):

Mean improvement: +0.0063 Pearson (95% CI: [+0.0043, +0.0090]).
Paired t-test: t = 4.70, p = 0.0054; Wilcoxon signed-rank: W = 21, p = 0.0313.
Effect size: Cohen’s d = 1.92, Hedges’ g = 1.61.
Win Rate: 6/6 (100%). True anatomical coordinates consistently outperform scrambled coordinates.

E_1 vs Capacity-Matched Control (CM_1):

Mean improvement: +0.0051 Pearson (95% CI: [+0.0031, +0.0076]).
Paired t-test: t = 4.88, p = 0.0045; Wilcoxon: p = 0.0313.
Win Rate: 6/6 (100%). Gains are not merely an artifact of extra parameter capacity.

E_1 vs Baseline A_0:

Mean improvement: +0.0039 Pearson (95% CI: [-0.0016, +0.0108]).
Paired t-test: p = 0.283, Win Rate: 4/6. The overall gain against A_0 is driven predominantly by Mask 1000000 on Lead I (+0.0214), while other cells are near-zero ties.

5.12 10-Epoch learning dynamics trajectory UMAP embedding
To discover whether architectural paradigms follow fundamentally distinct optimization trajectories, we vectorize the entire 10-epoch validation loss and missing-lead Pearson curves into 20-dimensional time-series vectors and project them into a 2D UMAP manifold:


Code
import umap

piv_loss = epochs.pivot_table(index=['run_name', 'variant', 'factorial_mask', 'observed_lead'], columns='epoch', values='val_loss')
piv_pearson = epochs.pivot_table(index=['run_name', 'variant', 'factorial_mask', 'observed_lead'], columns='epoch', values='val_missing_pearson')
piv_all = pd.concat([piv_loss.add_prefix('loss_'), piv_pearson.add_prefix('pearson_')], axis=1).dropna()

reducer_traj = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=8, min_dist=0.2, random_state=42)
u_traj = reducer_traj.fit_transform(piv_all)

traj_df = piv_all.reset_index()[['run_name', 'variant', 'factorial_mask', 'observed_lead']]
traj_df['Trajectory_UMAP1'] = u_traj[:, 0]
traj_df['Trajectory_UMAP2'] = u_traj[:, 1]

fig_traj_umap = px.scatter(
    traj_df, x='Trajectory_UMAP1', y='Trajectory_UMAP2',

The original factorial queue used short screening runs. This chapter contains only the promoted longer-budget extensions. A 3-, 10-, and 15-epoch result for the same named architecture are different estimands because training budget and checkpoint selection changed. The longest result supersedes the shorter result for final ranking, but the shorter trajectory remains useful for diagnosing whether screening preserved the ordering.

The gain is not a uniform shift: QRS IoU is already near saturation and typically increases by only 0.0025–0.0075, whereas P/T IoU and boundary F1 improve much more. At 15 epochs, no configuration dominates every endpoint. On lead I, A0_wave_noSSL has the highest mean Pearson (0.7474) and best reconstruction loss (0.8377), while R7 has the best boundary F1 (0.8784) and T/QRS overlap. On lead II, physiology-informed R5 leads mean Pearson (0.7607), lower-tail Pearson (0.4304), mIoU (0.8627), macro F1 (0.9261), and boundary F1 (0.8886), but A0_wave_noSSL retains the best reconstruction loss (0.7625).
This is encouraging for R5 on lead II but is not a clean SSL win. The principal contrast A0 raw → A0+wavelet → A0+wavelet+SSL is incomplete because a matched 15-epoch A0+wavelet+SSL cell is absent. R5 changes the second view and training objective, so it cannot identify whether wavelets, SSL, or UEG phase caused the result. C1_E1 remains a complementarity control; it does not support treating E1 as an improved base architecture.
Until multiple seeds and external evaluation land, differences on the order of one or two thousandths are treated as ties rather than mechanistic proof.

title: 6  One-Lead ECG-AIM Convergence Extensions
text:
6.7 Metric-Space Convergence UMAP Manifolds
To visualize how training horizon (10-epoch screening versus 15-epoch extension) reorganizes model performance across the multi-dimensional validation landscape, we compute 2D and 3D UMAP embeddings over all 11 standardized validation and delineation endpoints:


Code
import umap
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import plotly.graph_objects as go

valid_conv_metrics = [c for c in metric_cols if completed[c].notna().sum() > 20 and completed[c].std() > 1e-6]
X_conv = completed[valid_conv_metrics].fillna(completed[valid_conv_metrics].median()).values
X_conv_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_conv)

reducer_conv_2d = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=6, min_dist=0.2, random_state=42)
u_conv_2d = reducer_conv_2d.fit_transform(X_conv_scaled)
completed["UMAP1"] = u_conv_2d[:, 0]
completed["UMAP2"] = u_conv_2d[:, 1]

fig_conv_umap2d = px.scatter(
    completed, x="UMAP1", y="UMAP2",
    color="expected_epochs", symbol="observed_lead",
    size="miou_wave", hover_name="run_name",
    hover_data=["val_missing_pearson", "val_recon_loss", "boundary_f1_smoke", "P_iou", "T_iou"],
    labels={"UMAP1": "Convergence Metric UMAP 1", "UMAP2": "Convergence Metric UMAP 2",
            "expected_epochs": "Epoch Budget", "observed_lead": "Observed Lead"},
    title="2D Metric-Space UMAP: Horizon (10e vs 15e) and Lead Segregation Across All 33 Convergence Runs"
)
fig_conv_umap2d.update_layout(height=580)
fig_conv_umap2d.show()

reducer_conv_3d = umap.UMAP(n_components=3, n_neighbors=6, min_dist=0.2, random_state=42)
u_conv_3d = reducer_conv_3d.fit_transform(X_conv_scaled)
completed["UMAP3D_1"] = u_conv_3d[:, 0]
completed["UMAP3D_2"] = u_conv_3d[:, 1]
completed["UMAP3D_3"] = u_conv_3d[:, 2]

fig_conv_umap3d = px.scatter_3d(
    completed, x="UMAP3D_1", y="UMAP3D_2", z="UMAP3D_3",
    color="expected_epochs", symbol="observed_lead",
    size="val_missing_pearson", hover_name="run_name",
    hover_data=["miou_wave", "boundary_f1_smoke", "val_recon_loss"],
    labels={"UMAP3D_1": "UMAP 1", "UMAP3D_2": "UMAP 2", "UMAP3D_3": "UMAP 3"},
    title="3D Metric-Space UMAP: Global Convergence Topography Across Extended Budgets"
)
fig_conv_umap3d.update_traces(marker=dict(opacity=0.85))
fig_conv_umap3d.update_layout(height=650)
fig_conv_umap3d.show()

6.9 Evidence ledger








Question
Current answer
Why




Does longer training matter?
Yes, descriptively
All ten matched lead/configuration cells improve on major reconstruction and delineation endpoints from 10 to 15 epochs.


Is R5 the best completed model?
Endpoint- and lead-dependent
Strongest broad lead-II profile; not best lead-I reconstruction and not universally best loss.


Does UEG phase beat Morlet phase?
Suggestive on lead II, unresolved
R5 exceeds C1_E1 on several metrics, but the comparison also crosses A0/E1 architecture and lacks repeated seeds.


Does SSL add value beyond a wavelet branch?
Not yet identified
The matched 15-epoch A0+wavelet+SSL cell is missing.


Can validation select a clinical model?
No
Single seed, composite checkpoint selection, internal validation, and no paired per-record uncertainty.

title: 7  One-Lead ECG-AIM External RDB Evaluation
text:
7.1 Protocol boundary and dataset identity
This evaluation tests the 60 completed one-lead ECG-AIM spatial models on the external Russian Database (RDB) cohort.
RDB provides ground-truth clinical delineations for six distinct cardiac fiducials: - P-wave onset (P_{\text{onset}}) and offset (P_{\text{offset}}) - QRS-complex onset (QRS_{\text{onset}}) and offset (QRS_{\text{offset}}) - T-wave onset (T_{\text{onset}}) and offset (T_{\text{offset}})
No peak fiducials exist in the annotation protocol; hence, peak-based timing is not inferred or interpolated.

title: 7  One-Lead ECG-AIM External RDB Evaluation
text:
7.3 Six-boundary clinical delineation radar profiles
To assess whether spatial conditioning improves specific cardiac phases, we evaluate micro-averaged F1 score within a strict 20-ms clinical tolerance window across all six fiducial boundaries:


Code
boundary_focus = boundaries[(boundaries["stage"] == STAGE) & (boundaries["lead_group"] == LEAD_GROUP)].copy()
boundary_focus["variant"] = boundary_focus.model_id.str.extract(r"spatial_1lead_(.+)_\d{7}_s\d+_l[01]$")[0]

boundary_matrix = boundary_focus.groupby(["variant", "boundary"])["micro_f1_20ms"].mean().unstack()

fig_b_radar = go.Figure()
boundaries_order = ["P_onset", "P_offset", "QRS_onset", "QRS_offset", "T_onset", "T_offset"]
key_variants = ["a0", "e1_panorama_film", "cm1_capacity_matched", "pg1_permuted_geometry", "b1_panorama", "d1_panorama_relative"]

for var in key_variants:
    if var in boundary_matrix.index:
        vals = [boundary_matrix.loc[var, b] for b in boundaries_order]
        vals += [vals[0]]
        fig_b_radar.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar(
            r=vals, theta=boundaries_order + [boundaries_order[0]],
            fill='toself', name=var, opacity=0.25
        ))

fig_b_radar.update_layout(
    polar=dict(radialaxis=dict(visible=True, range=[0.4, 0.9])),
    title="Six-Boundary Delineation 20-ms Micro-F1 Profiles Across Key Architectures",
    height=600
)
fig_b_radar.show()


                            
                                            



7.3.1 Boundary-Specific Insights:

QRS Fiducials are Highly Preserved: Both QRS_{\text{onset}} and QRS_{\text{offset}} achieve 0.78–0.86 F1, reflecting steep, high-frequency voltage transitions that are robust to reconstruction blur.
P-Wave Boundaries Suffer Major Degradation: P_{\text{onset}} (0.45–0.54 F1) and P_{\text{offset}} (0.50–0.58 F1) exhibit substantial localization error due to low atrial depolarization amplitudes.
No Uniform Architectural Separation: Spatial variants like E_1 do not pull away from A_0 across boundaries; differences are confined to narrow \pm 0.01–0.02 bands.

7.4 Matched-event MAE versus 20-ms tolerance F1 landscape


Code
fig_mae_f1 = px.scatter(
    boundary_focus, x="mae_ms", y="micro_f1_20ms", color="boundary",
    symbol="variant", hover_name="model_id",
    hover_data=["bias_ms", "p95_abs_ms", "sensitivity_20ms", "ppv_20ms"],
    labels={"mae_ms": "Matched-Event MAE (ms, 150-ms window)", "micro_f1_20ms": "20-ms Strict Tolerance Micro-F1"},
    title="Fiducial Error Landscape: Matched-Event Precision versus Detection F1"
)
fig_mae_f1.update_layout(height=600)
fig_mae_f1.show()


                            
                                            


The error landscape illustrates two distinct failure mechanisms: 1. P-wave onset and offset cluster in the lower-right (high MAE >20 ms, lower F1 ~0.50). 2. QRS onset and offset cluster in the upper-left (low MAE ~10–14 ms, high F1 ~0.80–0.85).

7.5 Signed fiducial bias: Systematic onset advance versus offset delay


Code
fig_bias = px.box(
    boundary_focus, x="boundary", y="bias_ms", color="boundary",
    points="all", hover_name="model_id",
    labels={"bias_ms": "Signed Timing Bias (ms, Pred − Truth)", "boundary": "Cardiac Boundary"},
    title="Systematic Fiducial Timing Bias Across Reconstructed Waveforms"
)
fig_bias.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black")

P_{\text{onset}} displays a positive bias (+8 to +14 ms), indicating delayed onset detection.
T_{\text{offset}} displays negative bias (-4 to -12 ms), indicating premature repolarization truncation caused by low-amplitude signal smoothing in the autoencoder.

7.7 Bland-Altman reconstructed waveform agreement (in millivolts)


Code
signal_focus = signals[(signals["stage"] == STAGE) & (signals["lead_group"] == LEAD_GROUP)].copy()
signal_focus["variant"] = signal_focus.model_id.str.extract(r"spatial_1lead_(.+)_\d{7}_s\d+_l[01]$")[0]
signal_focus["loa_plus"] = signal_focus["loa_upper_mv"] - signal_focus["bias_mv"]
signal_focus["loa_minus"] = signal_focus["bias_mv"] - signal_focus["loa_lower_mv"]

fig_ba = px.scatter(
    signal_focus, x="bias_mv", y="record_pearson_mean",
    error_x="loa_plus", error_x_minus="loa_minus",
    color="variant", hover_name="model_id",
    labels={"bias_mv": "Waveform Amplitude Bias (mV)", "record_pearson_mean": "Mean Record Pearson Correlation"},
    title="Bland-Altman Voltage Agreement: Mean Bias and 95% Limits of Agreement (mV)"
)
fig_ba.add_vline(x=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black")
fig_ba.update_layout(height=550)
fig_ba.show()


                            
                                            


Waveform amplitude bias remains tightly centered around zero (\pm 0.005 mV), but the 95% Limits of Agreement span \pm 0.35 to \pm 0.50 mV across missing leads, demonstrating substantial voltage uncertainty on difficult pathological peaks.

text:
7.11 Global 2D & 3D Metric-Space External UMAP Manifolds
To construct an unbiased topological map of all 60 external models across the complete 32-dimensional evaluation matrix (comprising 6-boundary F1s, 6-boundary MAEs, P/QRS/T Dice & IoUs, signal Pearson mean & P05, MSE mean & P95, voltage bias, and Bland-Altman LoA span), we compute non-linear UMAP manifold projections:


Code
import umap
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

bnd_full = boundaries[(boundaries["stage"] == STAGE) & (boundaries["lead_group"] == LEAD_GROUP)].copy()
sig_full = signals[(signals["stage"] == STAGE) & (signals["lead_group"] == LEAD_GROUP)].copy()
reg_full = regions[(regions["stage"] == STAGE) & (regions["lead_group"] == LEAD_GROUP)].copy()

bnd_piv = bnd_full.pivot(index="model_id", columns="boundary", values=["micro_f1_20ms", "mae_ms"])
bnd_piv.columns = [f"{c[0]}_{c[1]}" for c in bnd_piv.columns]

reg_piv = reg_full.pivot(index="model_id", columns="wave", values=["dice", "iou"])
reg_piv.columns = [f"{c[0]}_{c[1]}" for c in reg_piv.columns]

sig_idx = sig_full.set_index("model_id")[["record_pearson_mean", "record_pearson_p05", "record_mse_mean", "record_mse_p95", "bias_mv"]]
sig_idx["loa_width_mv"] = sig_full.set_index("model_id")["loa_upper_mv"] - sig_full.set_index("model_id")["loa_lower_mv"]

ext_joined = full_evaluations.set_index("model_id").join(bnd_piv).join(reg_piv).join(sig_idx).reset_index()
metric_features = ext_joined.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns.tolist()
# Drop categorical index columns
metric_features = [c for c in metric_features if c not in ["input_lead", "attempts", "records"]]

X_ext = ext_joined[metric_features].fillna(ext_joined[metric_features].median()).values
X_ext_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_ext)

reducer_ext_2d = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=8, min_dist=0.2, random_state=42)
u_ext_2d = reducer_ext_2d.fit_transform(X_ext_scaled)
ext_joined["UMAP1"] = u_ext_2d[:, 0]
ext_joined["UMAP2"] = u_ext_2d[:, 1]

fig_ext_umap2d = px.scatter(
    ext_joined, x="UMAP1", y="UMAP2",
    color="factorial_mask", symbol="variant",
    size="primary_mean_micro_f1_20ms", hover_name="model_id",
    hover_data=["input_lead", "primary_signal_pearson_p05", "record_pearson_mean"],
    labels={"UMAP1": "External Metric UMAP 1", "UMAP2": "External Metric UMAP 2",
            "factorial_mask": "Factorial Mask", "variant": "Spatial Variant"},
    title="2D Metric-Space UMAP: Global Topological Structure Across All 60 External RDB Models"
)
fig_ext_umap2d.update_layout(height=600)
fig_ext_umap2d.show()

reducer_ext_3d = umap.UMAP(n_components=3, n_neighbors=8, min_dist=0.2, random_state=42)
u_ext_3d = reducer_ext_3d.fit_transform(X_ext_scaled)
ext_joined["UMAP3D_1"] = u_ext_3d[:, 0]
ext_joined["UMAP3D_2"] = u_ext_3d[:, 1]
ext_joined["UMAP3D_3"] = u_ext_3d[:, 2]

fig_ext_umap3d = px.scatter_3d(
    ext_joined, x="UMAP3D_1", y="UMAP3D_2", z="UMAP3D_3",
    color="factorial_mask", symbol="variant",
    size="primary_signal_pearson_p05", hover_name="model_id",
    hover_data=["primary_mean_micro_f1_20ms", "input_lead"],
    labels={"UMAP3D_1": "UMAP 1", "UMAP3D_2": "UMAP 2", "UMAP3D_3": "UMAP 3"},
    title="3D Metric-Space UMAP: Manifold Landscape Across 32 External Performance Dimensions"
)

section: 7.14 External spatial control transport testing: Where internal gains fail
text:
7.14 External spatial control transport testing: Where internal gains fail
To formally test why E_1 cannot be promoted as an improved universal base, we compute matched paired contrasts on the external RDB benchmark:


Code
ext_matrix = full_evaluations.pivot_table(
    index=["factorial_mask", "input_lead"], columns="variant",
    values=["primary_mean_micro_f1_20ms", "primary_signal_pearson_p05"]
)

transport_tests = []
for metric, metric_name in [("primary_mean_micro_f1_20ms", "Boundary F1 20ms"),
                            ("primary_signal_pearson_p05", "Signal Pearson P05")]:
    for cand, ref, label in [
        ("e1_panorama_film", "pg1_permuted_geometry", "E1 vs Permuted Geometry"),
        ("e1_panorama_film", "cm1_capacity_matched", "E1 vs Capacity Control"),
        ("e1_panorama_film", "a0", "E1 vs Baseline A0"),
        ("b1_panorama", "a0", "B1 vs Baseline A0"),
    ]:
        diffs = ext_matrix[(metric, cand)] - ext_matrix[(metric, ref)]
        diffs = diffs.dropna()
        n = len(diffs)
        mean_d = float(diffs.mean())
        std_d = float(diffs.std(ddof=1)) if n > 1 else 0.0
        t_stat, p_val = stats.ttest_1samp(diffs, 0.0) if n > 1 and std_d > 0 else (np.nan, np.nan)
        transport_tests.append({
            "metric": metric_name, "contrast": label,
            "mean_delta": mean_d, "std_delta": std_d,
            "ci_low": mean_d - 1.96 * (std_d / np.sqrt(n)),
            "ci_high": mean_d + 1.96 * (std_d / np.sqrt(n)),
            "p_value": p_val,
            "wins": int((diffs > 0).sum()), "losses": int((diffs < 0).sum()),
        })

df_ext_tests = pd.DataFrame(transport_tests)
display(df_ext_tests)

fig_ext_forest = go.Figure()
for idx, row in df_ext_tests.iterrows():
    fig_ext_forest.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=[row["mean_delta"]], y=[f"{row['metric']} · {row['contrast']}"],
        error_x=dict(type="data", symmetric=False,
                     array=[row["ci_high"] - row["mean_delta"]],
                     arrayminus=[row["mean_delta"] - row["ci_low"]],
                     width=6, thickness=2),
        mode="markers", marker=dict(size=10, color="teal" if row["mean_delta"] > 0 else "crimson"),
        name=row["contrast"],
        hovertext=f"Mean Δ: {row['mean_delta']:.4f}<br>95% CI: [{row['ci_low']:.4f}, {row['ci_high']:.4f}]<br>p-value: {row['p_value']:.4f}<br>Wins: {row['wins']}/6",
        hoverinfo="text"
    ))

fig_ext_forest.add_vline(x=0, line_dash="dash", line_color="black")
fig_ext_forest.update_layout(
    title="External RDB Matched Spatial Contrasts Forest Plot (95% CI)",
    xaxis_title="External Improvement (Δ on RDB)",
    yaxis=dict(autorange="reversed"),
    showlegend=False, height=500
)
fig_ext_forest.show()

7.14.1 Critical Transport Findings:

E_1 Geometry Advantage Reverses Externally:

For Boundary F1, E_1 - PG_1 averages +0.007 (p = 0.35), with losses in 2 out of 6 cells.
For Signal Pearson P05, E_1 - PG_1 averages -0.004 (p = 0.70), with 3 losses and 3 wins.

E_1 vs Capacity Control (CM_1) Fails Significance:

Boundary F1: p = 0.44; Signal P05: p = 0.84.

Conclusion: While true geometry provides a statistically significant +0.0063 gain on internal validation data, this advantage dissipates and reverses sign across external RDB cells. E_1 is therefore not an improved universal base.

shared = (le.query("model_id != '__original__'")
          .merge(re.query("model_id != '__original__'"), on="model_id",
                 suffixes=("_ludb", "_rdb")))
shared_metrics = ["signal_pearson_p05", "signal_mse_p95",
                  "primary_mean_micro_f1_20ms"]
transport_rows = []
for metric in shared_metrics:
    pair = shared[[f"{metric}_ludb", f"{metric}_rdb"]].dropna()
    transport_rows.append({
        "metric": metric, "shared_models": len(pair),
        "Pearson": pair.iloc[:, 0].corr(pair.iloc[:, 1]),
        "Spearman": pair.iloc[:, 0].corr(pair.iloc[:, 1], method="spearman")})
display(pd.DataFrame(transport_rows))

                 y="primary_mean_micro_f1_20ms_rdb", hover_name="model_id",

Boundary ranking transports moderately well: Spearman correlation is 0.736 across the 31 shared trained models. Waveform-tail ranking transports much less well: Pearson-p05 Spearman is 0.300 and MSE-p95 Spearman is −0.026. Dataset differences reorder models far more strongly for waveform fidelity than for downstream delineation retention.
This comparison is conditional on promotion. The 31 RDB models are a selected subset of the 123 LUDB candidates, so the correlation does not estimate transport for the full architecture space and may be range-restricted.

8.6 Retention relative to the measured-signal reference


Code
reference_rows = []
for cohort, frame in [("LUDB", le), ("RDB", re)]:
    reference = frame.query("model_id == '__original__'").iloc[0]
    trained = frame.query("model_id != '__original__'")
    for metric in shared_metrics:
        direction = metric_direction(metric)
        best = trained.sort_values(metric, ascending=(direction == "min")).iloc[0]
        favorable_gap = ((reference[metric] - best[metric]) if direction == "min"
                         else (best[metric] - reference[metric]))
        reference_rows.append({"cohort": cohort, "metric": metric,
                               "reference": reference[metric],
                               "best_model": best.model_id,
                               "best_reconstruction": best[metric],
                               "favorable_gap_vs_reference": favorable_gap})

On RDB, the best reconstructed boundary result is 0.7404 versus 0.7430 on the measured signal, a gap of 0.0026. On LUDB, the best reconstruction is 0.6302 versus 0.6938, a gap of 0.0636. The smaller RDB gap is encouraging for retaining the downstream delineator’s events, but does not mean the true waveform was recovered: RDB signal Pearson p05 remains at most 0.638.
The measured-signal row is a protocol reference, not a trainable competitor. Its Pearson of 1 and MSE of 0 are identities, while its boundary F1 is below 1 because the fixed delineator itself is imperfect. Boundary retention can approach the reference even when waveform fidelity remains limited.

8.9 Remaining limits
Principal checkpoints use seed 42. Cohorts have different annotations and distributions, and the RDB subset was selected rather than exhaustive. Aggregate summaries do not provide paired uncertainty for every model contrast. These results support external morphology-retention and failure-analysis claims, not clinical equivalence or waveform identifiability.

title: 9  Completed ECG-AIM Representation Study
text:
9.1 What question this study can answer
This is a frozen-representation audit, not another reconstruction leaderboard. It asks whether a frozen ECG-AIM encoder contains linearly accessible rhythm-code or annotation-timing information; whether that information adds to deliberately small waveform controls; whether 1011011 improves on the raw 1000000 anchor on the same records; and whether latent outliers are associated with reconstruction failure.
The rhythm endpoint is released cross-sectional code membership. The timing endpoint is the annotation interval from QRS onset to T offset; it is explicitly not clinical QT or QTc. Neither endpoint establishes diagnosis, prospective AF prediction, causal physiology, or identifiability of a missing 12-lead ECG.

title: 9  Completed ECG-AIM Representation Study
text:
ImportantBottom line



The latents contain useful rhythm-code information, but the current experiment does not show that 1011011 is a better AF representation than 1000000. 1011011 improves several measures of annotation-interval encoding, while direct waveform summaries remain substantially better for absolute timing. Rhythm codes are locally enriched in latent space but not globally separated.

All 11 extraction jobs are complete. Only the two anchors have train, validation, and test activations. Their probes were selected on validation data and evaluated once on shared test records. The other nine checkpoints are test-only and contribute geometry, similarity, and visualization—not fitted probes. Fitting probes on them would leak the evaluation split.
The pipeline standardizes and fits PCA on training data, restricts probes to at most eight PCA components, applies a validation one-standard-error selection rule favouring simpler candidates, and refits on train plus validation. Test intervals use paired record-level bootstrap resamples. These safeguards do not remove single-split or single-seed uncertainty.

The held-out set contains 120 AF/AFIB-coded and 240 other records. AUROC is not prevalence-dependent, but AUPRC must be interpreted against the 0.333 no-skill prevalence. The calibrated probes all select C=0.01; waveform uses three features and latent/combined probes use eight PCA dimensions. Strong shrinkage and low dimension make this closer to a linear-accessibility test than a large downstream classifier.
Test calibration slopes are 1.17–1.24 for latent-only and 1.10–1.15 for the combined probes, with intercepts near zero. This is reasonable internal calibration after validation adjustment, not external calibration. The 1011011 latent produces a larger interquartile predicted-risk contrast (0.302) than waveform summaries (0.186), but risk spread is not clinical net benefit.
The older probe_results table stores a superseded uncalibrated analysis with different selected regularization. This chapter consistently uses extended_results and its paired tables; mixing generations would change the estimand silently.

Adding latent features to waveform summaries improves AUROC by 0.0801 and AUPRC by 0.0788. Once the latent is present, adding the waveform summaries changes AUROC by only 0.0063 (CI crosses zero).

The defensible claim is incremental rhythm-code information, with stronger evidence for probability quality than for a large discrimination gain. Per-SD probe-score odds ratios near 3 are associations, not causal risks or prospective recurrence effects.

Adding either latent to waveform changes MAE by less than 0.24 ms, with intervals crossing zero. The latent does not add convincing absolute-timing utility beyond the waveform summaries.
The matched anchor contrast is more favourable: 1011011 reduces latent-only RMSE by 4.02 ms (95% CI 1.39–6.60; p=0.005), increases Spearman correlation by 0.109 (p=0.012), and increases Lin’s concordance by 0.108 (p=0.003). Its 2.42-ms MAE improvement narrowly includes zero (p=0.051). This supports better encoding of the annotation interval—not replacement of waveform timing and not a QT/QTc claim.

The enhanced anchor descriptively improves macro AUROC from 0.687 to 0.743 and macro F1 from 0.239 to 0.284, but balanced accuracy remains only 0.302. This is not an eight-class rhythm solution. Rare-code results are exploratory at 360 test records and must be shown class by class rather than summarized by the more flattering macro AUROC.
The test composition is deliberately uneven: AF, AFIB, SA, SB, and SR each have 60 records, while AT has 18 and ST/SVT have 21 each. The row-normalized confusion matrices show whether macro changes arise from common or rare codes. Specificity can remain high for a rare one-versus-rest class despite poor sensitivity, so neither specificity nor macro AUROC is sufficient alone.

section: 9.13 Spectral Disentanglement, Effective Rank, and Feature Redundancy
text:
9.13 Spectral Disentanglement, Effective Rank, and Feature Redundancy
Inspired by recent advances in frequency-aware ECG foundation models (such as ECG-Nest-FM, Sharma et al., 2025; Balestriero et al., 2023; Garrido et al., 2023), we conduct a rigorous mathematical investigation of the internal structure, spectral entropy, dimensional collapse, and feature redundancy of our frozen encoder representations.

9.13.1 Mathematical Framework

Average Absolute Cross-Correlation: \text{Cross-Corr}(Z) = \frac{1}{|U|} \sum_{i < j} |R_{ij}| where R \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D} is the Pearson correlation matrix of the D = 2304 representation features across evaluated patient records, and U is the set of off-diagonal index pairs. Lower values indicate greater feature decorrelation and lower representation redundancy.
Spectral Entropy & Smooth Effective Rank (SER): Given the centered representation matrix Z \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D} with singular values \sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_K > 0, the normalized singular value distribution is: p_k = \frac{\sigma_k}{\sum_{i=1}^K \sigma_i} The singular value spectral entropy and Smooth Effective Rank are defined as: H(p) = -\sum_{k=1}^K p_k \log p_k, \qquad \text{SER} = \exp(H(p)) SER quantifies the effective dimensionality occupied by the representations. A higher SER indicates that the representations span a diverse, high-rank latent subspace without dimensional collapse (Roy & Vetterli, 2007).
Physiological Frequency Hierarchies: ECG signals exhibit canonical frequency bands tied to cardiac electrophysiology:

0–10 Hz (Low Frequency): T-wave repolarization, baseline hemodynamics, and heart rate.
5–30 Hz (Mid Frequency): P-wave atrial depolarization and Atrial Fibrillation fibrillatory dynamics (4–9 Hz).
8–50 Hz (High Frequency): QRS complex rapid ventricular depolarization and conduction delays (LBBB, RBBB).




Code
import sqlite3, zlib, numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import svd

# Connect and extract feature arrays across all 11 models
svd_data = []
ser_records = []

for idx, job in jobs.iterrows():
    job_id = job["job_id"]
    m_id = job["model_id"].replace("factorial_ecg_aim_", "")
    rows = read_sql(DB, f"select record_id, dim, dtype, compression, feature_blob from features where job_id = '{job_id}'")
    if rows.empty:
        continue
    
    feats = [np.frombuffer(zlib.decompress(r["feature_blob"]) if r["compression"] == "zlib" else r["feature_blob"], dtype=r["dtype"]) for _, r in rows.iterrows()]
    X = np.array(feats, dtype=np.float32)
    N, D = X.shape
    
    # Feature centering and standardization
    X_cent = X - X.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    std = X_cent.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    std[std == 0] = 1.0
    X_norm = X_cent / std
    
    # Subsampled pairwise cross-correlation (300 uniform features)
    idx_feat = np.linspace(0, D - 1, 300, dtype=int)
    corr = np.corrcoef(X_norm[:, idx_feat].T)
    off_diag = corr[np.triu_indices(len(idx_feat), k=1)]
    valid_off_diag = off_diag[~np.isnan(off_diag)]
    avg_abs_corr = float(np.mean(np.abs(valid_off_diag)))
    
    # SVD on centered representations
    U, s, Vt = svd(X_cent, full_matrices=False)
    s_norm = s / (np.sum(s) + 1e-12)
    s_norm_pos = s_norm[s_norm > 1e-12]
    spectral_entropy = float(-np.sum(s_norm_pos * np.log(s_norm_pos)))
    ser = float(np.exp(spectral_entropy))
    
    ser_records.append({
        "Model Config": m_id,
        "Records (N)": N,
        "Dim (D)": D,
        "Avg Abs Cross-Corr": round(avg_abs_corr, 4),
        "Spectral Entropy": round(spectral_entropy, 3),
        "Smooth Effective Rank (SER)": round(ser, 2)
    })
    
    for k_idx, s_val in enumerate(s_norm[:150]):
        svd_data.append({
            "model_id": m_id,
            "singular_value_index": k_idx + 1,
            "log10_normalized_singular_value": float(np.log10(s_val + 1e-12)),
            "normalized_singular_value": float(s_val)
        })

df_ser_table = pd.DataFrame(ser_records)
df_svd_all = pd.DataFrame(svd_data)

9.13.4 Nested / Truncated Sub-Dimensionality Probing
To test whether early dimensions capture lower-frequency rhythm dynamics (AF, 4–9 Hz) before higher dimensions capture fine temporal conduction (QRS interval timing, 8–50 Hz), we evaluate linear probe performance as a function of truncated latent dimensions D \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024\}:


Code
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, r2_score

nested_probing_results = []

for idx, job in jobs[jobs.model_id.isin(ANCHORS)].iterrows():
    job_id = job["job_id"]
    m_id = job["model_id"].replace("factorial_ecg_aim_", "")
    rows = read_sql(DB, f"select record_id, dim, dtype, compression, feature_blob from features where job_id = '{job_id}'")
    feats = {r["record_id"]: np.frombuffer(zlib.decompress(r["feature_blob"]) if r["compression"] == "zlib" else r["feature_blob"], dtype=r["dtype"]) for _, r in rows.iterrows()}
    
    df_m = records[records.record_id.isin(feats.keys())].copy()
    X_all = np.array([feats[rid] for rid in df_m.record_id], dtype=np.float32)
    y_af = (df_m.canonical_rhythm == "AFIB").astype(int).values
    y_timing = df_m.qrson_toff_ms.values
    splits = df_m.split.values
    
    train_mask = (splits == "train") | (splits == "val")
    test_mask = (splits == "test")
    
    X_train = X_all[train_mask]
    X_test = X_all[test_mask]
    y_af_train, y_af_test = y_af[train_mask], y_af[test_mask]
    
    # Non-null timing masks
    t_train_valid = train_mask & (~np.isnan(y_timing))
    t_test_valid = test_mask & (~np.isnan(y_timing))
    
    # Standardization & PCA
    mean = X_train.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    std = X_train.std(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    std[std == 0] = 1.0
    X_train_norm = (X_train - mean) / std
    X_test_norm = (X_test - mean) / std
    
    U, s, Vt = svd(X_train_norm, full_matrices=False)
    X_train_pca = np.dot(X_train_norm, Vt.T)
    X_test_pca = np.dot(X_test_norm, Vt.T)
    X_all_pca = np.dot((X_all - mean) / std, Vt.T)
    
    dims_to_test = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]
    for d in dims_to_test:
        if d > X_train_pca.shape[1]: continue
        
        # Atrial Fibrillation Probe (Logistic Regression)
        clf = LogisticRegression(C=0.01, max_iter=1000, random_state=42)
        clf.fit(X_train_pca[:, :d], y_af_train)
        preds_af = clf.predict_proba(X_test_pca[:, :d])[:, 1]
        auroc = roc_auc_score(y_af_test, preds_af)
        
        # QRS Timing Interval Probe (Ridge Regression)
        reg = Ridge(alpha=10.0)
        reg.fit(X_all_pca[t_train_valid, :d], y_timing[t_train_valid])
        preds_t = reg.predict(X_all_pca[t_test_valid, :d])
        r2 = r2_score(y_timing[t_test_valid], preds_t)
        
        nested_probing_results.append({
            "model_id": m_id,
            "dims": d,
            "AF AUROC": auroc,
            "QRS Timing R2": r2
        })

df_nested = pd.DataFrame(nested_probing_results)

fig_nested_af = px.line(
    df_nested, x="dims", y="AF AUROC", color="model_id", markers=True,
    labels={"dims": "Truncated Embedding Dimensions (d)", "AF AUROC": "Held-Out AF AUROC"},
    title="Nested Representation Scaling: AF Discrimination Capacity vs Sub-Embedding Dimension"
)
fig_nested_af.update_xaxes(type="log", dtick=1)
fig_nested_af.update_layout(height=450)
fig_nested_af.show()

)

text:
9.14 Clinically-Guided Contrastive Geometry (CLEF-Inspired Analysis)
Following the clinically-guided representation learning paradigm established by CLEF (Shu et al., UCL / Nokia Bell Labs / Tampere University, ICLR 2026 under review, arXiv:2512.02180), we interrogate whether self-supervised ECG foundation representations align their latent geometry with clinical metadata, pathology superclasses, and continuous physiological intervals.

9.14.1 Theoretical Foundation: Contrastive Geometry & Dissimilarity Alignment
In the CLEF framework, the continuous clinical dissimilarity \delta_{ik} between subjects i and k is mapped into a pairwise adaptive negative weighting: W_{ik} = D_{ik} \cdot M_{ik} \in [0, 1] where D_{ik} = (1-\alpha)\frac{\delta_{ik} - \delta_{\min}}{\delta_{\max} - \delta_{\min}} + \alpha and M_{ik} = \exp\left(-\frac{A - m_i}{A} \times \frac{A - m_k}{A}\right) accounts for metadata completeness across A clinical attributes.
The resulting normalized cosine similarity \hat{S}_{ij} = \frac{1 + f_{\text{sim}}(z_i, z_j)}{2} is aligned with clinical dissimilarity via the L_d alignment objective: \mathcal{L}_d = \frac{1}{B^2} \sum_{i,j} \left( \hat{S}_{ij} - (1 - W_{ij}) \right)^2
To evaluate the degree of clinical alignment learned across all 11 factorial model checkpoints, we compute: 1. Intra-class vs. Inter-class Cosine Similarity Separation: \Delta S = \mathbb{E}[S_{\text{intra}}] - \mathbb{E}[S_{\text{inter}}], \quad F_{\text{ratio}} = \frac{(\mathbb{E}[S_{\text{intra}}] - \mathbb{E}[S_{\text{inter}}])^2}{\text{Var}(S_{\text{intra}}) + \text{Var}(S_{\text{inter}})} 2. Physiological Metric Space Alignment (r_s): Spearman rank correlation between embedding cosine distance 1 - f_{\text{sim}}(z_i, z_j) and physiological difference \Delta \text{Physiology}_{ij} across Heart Rate (\Delta \text{bpm}), Rhythm Irregularity (\Delta \text{RR-CV}), Conduction/Repolarization Duration (\Delta QRS_{\text{on}}\text{--}T_{\text{off}} ms), and Spectral Complexity (\Delta \text{Entropy}).


Code
# Extract all model embeddings and compute CLEF geometry metrics
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
clef_records = records.set_index("record_id")
features_all = read_sql(DB, "select job_id, record_id, feature_blob from features")

feats_by_job = {}
for jid, group in features_all.groupby("job_id"):
    rids = group["record_id"].tolist()
    blobs = [np.frombuffer(zlib.decompress(b), dtype=np.float16).astype(np.float32) for b in group["feature_blob"]]
    feats_by_job[jid] = pd.DataFrame(blobs, index=rids)

clef_table_data = []
clef_scatter_data = {}

for _, j in jobs.iterrows():
    jid = j["job_id"]
    mid = j["model_id"].replace("factorial_ecg_aim_", "")
    df_f = feats_by_job[jid]
    common = df_f.index.intersection(clef_records.index)
    df_f = df_f.loc[common]
    df_r = clef_records.loc[common]
    
    valid_mask = df_r["heart_rate_bpm"].notna() & df_r["rr_cv"].notna() & df_r["qrson_toff_ms"].notna() & df_r["spectral_entropy"].notna()
    df_f_v = df_f[valid_mask]
    df_r_v = df_r[valid_mask]
    
    # Stratified subset across rhythm classes
    stratified_ids = df_r_v.groupby("canonical_rhythm", group_keys=False).apply(lambda x: x.sample(min(len(x), 40), random_state=42)).index
    
    X_sub = df_f_v.loc[stratified_ids].values
    r_sub = df_r_v.loc[stratified_ids]
    
    norm_X = X_sub / (np.linalg.norm(X_sub, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-8)
    cos_sim = np.dot(norm_X, norm_X.T)
    cos_dist = 1.0 - cos_sim
    n_sample = len(stratified_ids)
    
    hr_dist = np.abs(r_sub["heart_rate_bpm"].values[:, None] - r_sub["heart_rate_bpm"].values[None, :])
    rr_dist = np.abs(r_sub["rr_cv"].values[:, None] - r_sub["rr_cv"].values[None, :])
    timing_dist = np.abs(r_sub["qrson_toff_ms"].values[:, None] - r_sub["qrson_toff_ms"].values[None, :])
    entropy_dist = np.abs(r_sub["spectral_entropy"].values[:, None] - r_sub["spectral_entropy"].values[None, :])
    
    i_upper = np.triu_indices(n_sample, k=1)
    hr_corr, _ = spearmanr(cos_dist[i_upper], hr_dist[i_upper])
    rr_corr, _ = spearmanr(cos_dist[i_upper], rr_dist[i_upper])
    timing_corr, _ = spearmanr(cos_dist[i_upper], timing_dist[i_upper])
    entropy_corr, _ = spearmanr(cos_dist[i_upper], entropy_dist[i_upper])
    
    rhythms = r_sub["canonical_rhythm"].values
    intra_sims, inter_sims = [], []
    for i in range(len(rhythms)):
        for k in range(i+1, len(rhythms)):
            if rhythms[i] == rhythms[k]:
                intra_sims.append(cos_sim[i, k])
            else:
                inter_sims.append(cos_sim[i, k])
    intra_m, intra_s = np.mean(intra_sims), np.std(intra_sims)
    inter_m, inter_s = np.mean(inter_sims), np.std(inter_sims)
    margin = intra_m - inter_m
    fisher = (margin**2) / (intra_s**2 + inter_s**2 + 1e-8)
    
    clef_table_data.append({
        "Model Checkpoint": mid,
        "Intra-Class Sim": f"{intra_m:.4f} ± {intra_s:.4f}",
        "Inter-Class Sim": f"{inter_m:.4f} ± {inter_s:.4f}",
        "Separation Margin (ΔS)": margin,
        "Fisher Ratio (F)": fisher,
        "HR Dist rs": hr_corr,
        "RR-CV Dist rs": rr_corr,
        "QRS-T Dist rs": timing_corr,
        "Entropy Dist rs": entropy_corr
    })
    
    if mid in ["1000000_s42", "1011011_s42", "1001014_s42", "1010010_s42"]:
        clef_scatter_data[mid] = {
            "cos_dist": cos_dist[i_upper],
            "hr_dist": hr_dist[i_upper],
            "timing_dist": timing_dist[i_upper],
            "intra_sims": intra_sims,
            "inter_sims": inter_sims
        }

df_clef_summary = pd.DataFrame(clef_table_data)
display(df_clef_summary)

title: 9  Completed ECG-AIM Representation Study
text:
9.16 What would change the conclusion
The highest-value follow-ups are repeated patient-level splits or external cohorts; a strong native-waveform classifier comparator; predeclared probe dimensionality; calibration and decision-curve analysis; external validation of the failure score; and matched one-lead wavelet representations once train/validation/test embeddings exist. Until then, this supports a representation-mechanism and quality-control claim, not deployment.

summary = (streams.groupby(["source", "run_id"])
           .agg(streams=("record_id", "size"), miou_mean=("miou", "mean"),
                miou_p05=("miou", lambda x: x.quantile(.05)),
                p_iou=("p_iou", "mean"), qrs_iou=("qrs_iou", "mean"),
                t_iou=("t_iou", "mean"), pr_error_ms=("notebook_pr_error_ms", "mean"),
                qrs_error_ms=("notebook_qrs_error_ms", "mean"),
                qt_error_ms=("notebook_qt_error_ms", "mean"))
           .reset_index())
summary = summary.merge(runs[["source", "run_id", "split", "state_name", "padding",
                              "checkpoint_sha256", "evaluator_sha256",
                              "metric.protocol", "metric.tolerance_ms",
                              "metric.evaluation_window"]],
                        on=["source", "run_id"], how="left")
display(summary)

# Boundary tolerance changes event matching but not region/interval predictions.
# Collapse exact performance duplicates before ranking those endpoints.
performance_columns = ["miou_mean", "miou_p05", "p_iou", "qrs_iou", "t_iou",
                       "pr_error_ms", "qrs_error_ms", "qt_error_ms"]
canonical_streams = summary.drop_duplicates(
    subset=["source", "checkpoint_sha256", "evaluator_sha256", "split",
            "state_name", "padding", *performance_columns]).copy()
display(leaderboard(canonical_streams, numeric_metrics(canonical_streams), id_col="run_id",
                    group_cols=("source",), k=10))

For the v1 test checkpoint, notebook padding changes foreground mIoU from 0.594 to 0.840 and reduces QT interval error from 30.45 to 11.34 ms—far larger than the EMA effect. This is not evidence that padding makes the learned model intrinsically better. It shows that temporal alignment and the evaluation window are part of the estimand. The v2 annotated window was introduced to make this contract explicit.
In the mean-teacher test package, notebook padding produces a smaller change (foreground mIoU 0.775 to 0.783), with the largest benefit in P-wave overlap and interval errors. Results from none, notebook, legacy v1, and annotated v2 must not be pooled into a single model leaderboard.

title: 10  Completed LUDB Semi-Supervised Delineation Results
text:
10.6 Wave-specific failure structure
Across the v2 mean-teacher test runs, QRS IoU is approximately 0.84, whereas P-wave IoU is about 0.67–0.71 and T-wave IoU about 0.80. QRS timing errors are roughly 8–9 ms, while PR and QT errors remain larger. The principal residual weakness is therefore atrial morphology and interval construction rather than QRS localization. A headline mIoU obscures that imbalance.

title: 10  Completed LUDB Semi-Supervised Delineation Results
text:
10.8 Remaining inferential limits
The databases contain a small number of checkpoint/state evaluations rather than replicated training seeds. Stream observations are clustered within 40 subjects, but the summary tables do not provide subject-bootstrap confidence intervals for student-versus-EMA or padding contrasts. Differences here are descriptive engineering evidence until repeated training and subject-level paired inference are added.

convergence["configuration"] = (convergence.run_name
    .str.replace(r"^conv(?:10|15)e_", "", regex=True)
    .str.replace(r"_s\d+_l[01]$", "", regex=True))

    id_vars=["configuration", "observed_lead", "expected_epochs", "run_name"],

title: 13  Seven-Character Factorial Reconstruction Results
text:
13.3 Factorial interpretation contract
The confirmatory analysis should estimate five binary main effects, four MMD contrasts against level zero, and prespecified interactions using paired records and seed blocks. It should not rank 160 cells and declare the maximum a discovery. The all-binary-on masks 1111110–1111114 form a kernel family; none is a generic “full loss” independent of kernel choice.

title: 13  Seven-Character Factorial Reconstruction Results
section: 13.4 What remains before a defensible result
text:
13.4 What remains before a defensible result

Finish the five MSVAE and 37 ECG-AIM checkpoint cells or explicitly freeze a reduced estimand.
Run identical, generation-bound missing-lead test inference.
Preserve per-record pairing and patient clustering.
Report optimization failures rather than silently dropping masks.
Treat U-Net validation patterns as hypothesis generation until replicated.

title: 14  Clinical Biomarker Preservation under missing_leads_v2
text:
14.1 Why missing_leads_v2 is canonical
This evaluation scores reconstructed missing leads against the measured 12-lead ECG and prevents observed-lead passthrough from inflating performance. Rows from legacy_v1 are not pooled with it. The reference rows describe the measured-signal benchmark; they are not trained reconstruction models.

title: 15  One-Lead Reconstruction: Architecture and Spatial Conditioning
text:
15.1 A distinct input contract and spatial projection problem
Single-lead ECG reconstruction presents an inherently underdetermined inverse problem: estimating 11 missing lead waveforms from a single observed lead (Lead I or Lead II).
Unlike 3-lead models (which observe Leads I, II, and V_2 simultaneously spanning both frontal and transverse planes), a 1-lead model observes only a single 1D projection of the 3D cardiac electrical dipole vector \mathbf{p}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^3: V_L(t) = \mathbf{c}_L \cdot \mathbf{p}(t) + \eta_L(t) where \mathbf{c}_L \in \mathbb{R}^3 represents the lead vector defined by lead electrode geometry.

15.3 Architectural taxonomy and spatial ablation tree
To evaluate whether neural networks can exploit these anatomical projection vectors, ten architectural conditioning variants were systematically formulated:

section: 15.6 Core mechanism questions and claim hierarchy
text:
15.6 Core mechanism questions and claim hierarchy

A0 \to Spatial Encoding: Does supplying explicit anatomical coordinates (\theta, \phi, z) improve missing-lead estimation over an unconditioned base?
True vs Permuted Geometry (E_1 vs PG_1): Does the network genuinely utilize physiological spatial relationships, or does any arbitrary positional embedding suffice?
Capacity Matching (E_1 vs CM_1): Are observed gains attributable to anatomical conditioning or simply increased parameter capacity?
Generalization & Transport: Do internal validation advantages persist on external cohorts (RDB)?

The empirical resolutions to these questions are detailed in: - Chapter 27: Comprehensive analysis of internal validation results and learning dynamics across all 60 runs. - Chapter 26: External validation on the 360-record Russian Database (RDB) cohort.

The causal ordering is:
A0 → A0 + wavelet → A0 + wavelet + SSL.
E1 is reserved for the matched complementarity contrast A0+wavelet+SSL versus E1+wavelet+SSL. This prevents architectural changes from being credited to wavelets or SSL.

title: 17  Evidence Synthesis and Run Gaps
text:
17.3 Integrated findings by scientific question

17.3.1 1. What is currently the strongest one-lead result?
There is no endpoint-independent winner. At 15 epochs, R5 (Morlet magnitude + UEG Wyatt phase) has the strongest broad lead-II profile: Pearson 0.7607, Pearson p05 0.4304, wave mIoU 0.8627, macro wave F1 0.9261, and boundary F1 0.8886. On lead I, the simpler A0 wavelet/no-SSL model retains the best mean Pearson and reconstruction loss, while R7 leads several boundary and T-wave endpoints. These are internal validation estimates, not external RDB rankings.
Externally, B1 panorama at mask 1010010 gives the best one-lead RDB boundary F1 on both observed leads (0.6585 lead I; 0.6742 lead II). Other spatial models lead waveform lower-tail metrics. Selecting “the best” therefore requires an intended endpoint: waveform similarity, difficult-record protection, event timing, or region overlap.


17.3.2 2. What do wavelets add?
The clean three-epoch A0 contrast shows that a wavelet branch primarily improves P/T delineation: P-wave IoU rises by 0.171 on lead I and 0.083 on lead II, whereas QRS IoU changes by only 0.001–0.003. This is consistent with the longer convergence data, where QRS is near saturation and additional epochs mostly improve P/T and boundaries. The cost is approximately 4.16 GB additional peak GPU memory at screening scale.
This supports a morphology-specific wavelet mechanism, but not yet a general clinical benefit. The wavelet checkpoints have not undergone the same external RDB protocol as the completed legacy spatial models.


17.3.3 3. What does SSL add?
At three epochs, adding SSL to the wavelet branch is neutral/slightly adverse on lead I and favourable for lead-II delineation, while adding about 8.45 GB peak memory. The 15-epoch generation lacks a matched A0+wavelet+SSL cell, so the registered A0 raw → A0+wavelet → A0+wavelet+SSL chain is not complete at the confirmatory horizon. R5 cannot isolate SSL because it changes the physiological view simultaneously. The honest conclusion is possible lead-specific complementarity, not an identified SSL main effect.


17.3.4 4. Does physiological geometry help?
Internally, true E1 geometry beats both permuted geometry and a capacity-matched control in all six mask×lead cells. However, E1 is nearly tied with A0 in five of those six cells. On external RDB, E1-control differences reverse sign across masks, leads, and endpoints. Correct geometry is used by the network, but the data do not support E1 as a generally improved base architecture or a robust external advantage.


17.3.5 5. What do the linear probes establish?
Frozen ECG-AIM latents contain AF/AFIB-code information beyond heart rate, RMS, and spectral entropy. The enhanced anchor’s latent AUROC is 0.787 versus 0.713 for waveform summaries, with calibrated-probability improvements surviving the prespecified correction. Yet 1011011 does not significantly beat 1000000 in direct paired AF metrics: the AUROC difference is +0.027 with a 95% interval from −0.023 to +0.076.
For annotation QRS-onset–to–T-offset duration, 1011011 improves latent-only RMSE and concordance relative to 1000000, but both latents are much worse than direct waveform summaries for absolute MAE. This is representation-content evidence, not diagnostic superiority or a clinical QT/QTc result.
High-dimensional tests find significant local rhythm-code neighbour enrichment but negative, non-significant silhouettes. UMAPs can illustrate local structure but cannot be described as globally separated rhythm manifolds.


17.3.6 6. How well do results transport?
Among the 31 shared three-lead models, LUDB-to-RDB boundary-F1 rank correlation is 0.736. Waveform-tail rank correlations are weak (0.300 for Pearson p05 and approximately zero for MSE p95). Boundary retention is therefore more stable than waveform-fidelity ranking.
For the 60 one-lead spatial models, internal validation correlates only moderately with full RDB endpoints. The 48-record RDB pilot predicts boundary ranking well enough for screening (Spearman 0.82–0.87) but predicts signal-p05 ranking poorly (0.45). Model promotion based on one surrogate will miss endpoint-specific external leaders.


17.3.7 7. Which apparent gains are evaluator effects?
LUDB semi-supervised results show that padding and evaluation-window choice can change foreground mIoU by roughly 0.25—orders of magnitude larger than the student-versus-EMA differences. Two tolerance rows also reuse identical region predictions. The checkpoint, state, split, padding, window, evaluator hash, and tolerance jointly define the estimand; rows differing only in event tolerance must not be counted as independent region evidence.

18.1 Evidence map
This is the first numbered chapter because every later result inherits its data contract. It replaces “representative synthetic ECG” reasoning with an auditable description of the data actually present in this repository. The analysis has three levels: metadata integrity, signal integrity, and task integrity. A reconstruction benchmark is only interpretable when all three hold.
Every executable audit below resolves its input beneath ../data/ and prints the resolved path. No waveform statistic in this chapter is generated from the later synthetic tutorials.
These artifacts do not support the same inference. PTB-XL is the reconstruction development cohort. EchoNext is an external transfer cohort with echocardiography-derived labels. Performance on EchoNext tests transport under a different sampling and normalization pipeline; it does not retroactively enlarge the PTB-XL training set.

18.2 PTB-XL: observed cohort and split contract
The local metadata contain 21,799 ECG records and 28 columns. The ten official stratification folds are nearly balanced (2,173–2,198 records each). The locked model registry maps folds 1–8 to training (17,418 records), fold 9 to validation (2,183), and fold 10 to test (2,198). The registry also reports 1,904 unique patients in the test set, so patient-clustered uncertainty is necessary: record-level resampling would treat repeated ECGs from the same person as independent.
The raw age field deserves an explicit validity audit. Its observed maximum is 300, which is not physiologically plausible as years and should not silently enter subgroup analysis. Age-based EDA must therefore report invalid-value counts and either use a documented correction supplied by the dataset or mark those values missing. It must not “fix” them by clipping without a sensitivity analysis.

18.2.3 Executed PTB-XL waveform audit
The following block reads the actual paired WFDB records named by filename_hr and filename_lr in data/ptb_xl/ptbxl_database.csv. To keep HTML rendering reproducible and bounded, it uses a fixed, fold-stratified audit sample of 25 records from each official fold (250 records total); this is an EDA sample, not an inferential subsample. Primary signal summaries use the stored 500 Hz physical waveforms. The paired 100 Hz releases are upsampled to quantify what a 100→500 Hz adapter can and cannot recover.


Code
import wfdb
from scipy.signal import resample_poly, welch

PTB_ROOT = (ROOT / "data/ptb_xl").resolve()
audit_rows = (
    ptb.groupby("strat_fold", group_keys=False)
       .sample(n=25, random_state=20260731)
       .sort_values(["strat_fold", "ecg_id"])
)
signals_hr = []
signals_lr_up = []
for row in audit_rows[["filename_hr", "filename_lr"]].itertuples(index=False):
    signal_hr, fields_hr = wfdb.rdsamp(str(PTB_ROOT / row.filename_hr))
    signal_lr, fields_lr = wfdb.rdsamp(str(PTB_ROOT / row.filename_lr))
    if fields_hr["fs"] != 500 or signal_hr.shape != (5000, 12):
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected PTB-XL high-resolution contract: {row.filename_hr}")
    if fields_lr["fs"] != 100 or signal_lr.shape != (1000, 12):
        raise ValueError(f"Unexpected PTB-XL low-resolution contract: {row.filename_lr}")
    if fields_hr["sig_name"] != fields_lr["sig_name"]:
        raise ValueError(f"Lead-order mismatch: {row.filename_hr} vs {row.filename_lr}")
    signals_hr.append(signal_hr.astype(np.float32))
    signals_lr_up.append(
        resample_poly(signal_lr, up=5, down=1, axis=0).astype(np.float32)
    )
ptb_wave = np.stack(signals_hr)  # records × 5000 samples × leads
ptb_lr_up = np.stack(signals_lr_up)
fields = fields_hr
lead_names = fields["sig_name"]

finite = np.isfinite(ptb_wave)
lead_sd = ptb_wave.std(axis=1)
freq, psd = welch(ptb_wave, fs=500, axis=1, nperseg=1024)
band_power = {
    "baseline_<0.5Hz": np.trapz(psd[:, (freq < 0.5), :], freq[freq < 0.5], axis=1),
    "cardiac_0.5-40Hz": np.trapz(
        psd[:, (freq >= 0.5) & (freq <= 40), :],
        freq[(freq >= 0.5) & (freq <= 40)], axis=1
    ),
    "high_40-150Hz": np.trapz(
        psd[:, (freq > 40) & (freq <= 150), :],
        freq[(freq > 40) & (freq <= 150)], axis=1
    ),
}

ptb_signal_audit = pd.DataFrame({
    "lead": lead_names,
    "finite_percent": 100 * finite.mean(axis=(0, 1)),
    "p01_mV": np.quantile(ptb_wave, 0.01, axis=(0, 1)),
    "median_mV": np.median(ptb_wave, axis=(0, 1)),
    "p99_mV": np.quantile(ptb_wave, 0.99, axis=(0, 1)),
    "median_RMS_mV": np.median(np.sqrt(np.mean(ptb_wave ** 2, axis=1)), axis=0),
    "near_flat_records_percent": 100 * (lead_sd < 1e-4).mean(axis=0),
    "median_high_frequency_fraction": np.median(
        band_power["high_40-150Hz"] /
        np.maximum(
            band_power["cardiac_0.5-40Hz"] + band_power["high_40-150Hz"],
            1e-12
        ),
        axis=0
    ),
})
print(f"Loaded {len(ptb_wave)} paired 500 Hz/100 Hz real records from {PTB_ROOT}")

Because 100 Hz data have a 50 Hz Nyquist limit, upsampling cannot restore true 40–150 Hz content present in the 500 Hz release. The paired error above measures the complete adapter discrepancy; final morphology analysis should additionally compare QRS-band power and fiducials before and after any model-specific resampling.


18.2.4 The actual model-input tensor boundary
Raw WFDB EDA is necessary but not sufficient: the reconstruction code does not read WFDB files during training. scripts/train_mcma_3lead.py::PTBXLDataset loads .pt files, expects shape 12 × 5000, appends 120 zeros to reach a pooling-compatible length of 5,120, and selects lead indices [0, 1, 7]—I, II, and V2—as the model input. Targets contain all 12 padded leads. The training loader applies no per-record standardization, filtering, or amplitude clipping.
The following audit is computed over every tensor, not the 250-record raw-waveform sample. To keep routine book renders tractable, scripts/audit_ptbxl_tensors_for_book.py performs the 5 GB sequential scan with the project venv and writes a record-level Parquet plus a JSON summary. Each tensor is loaded through torch.load(..., weights_only=True) and checked for metadata/split alignment, shape, dtype, nonfinite values, flat leads, amplitude, RMS, and SHA-256 of canonical float32 signal bytes.

The executed gate finds all 21,799 of 21,799 expected tensors in the correct split, all with shape 12 × 5000, dtype float32, finite values, and unique canonical signal hashes. It also finds one concrete quality exception: training ECG 12722 has an exactly zero V5 lead. That record should be retained in the cohort ledger and handled by an explicit quality policy, not silently disappear inside a data loader.
The gate distinguishes three failure classes. A missing tensor is a cohort-definition error; a malformed/nonfinite tensor is a preprocessing error; a duplicate canonical hash is a potential leakage or export error requiring record-level adjudication. A perfectly matched inventory does not by itself prove the correct physical units, so the next two checks inspect the distribution and pair tensors back to the raw 500 Hz waveforms.

18.3 EchoNext: population, waveform, and endpoint audit
The local EchoNext metadata table contains 100,000 records and 39 fields. The frozen external test array contains 5,442 × 1 × 2,500 × 12 values. At the declared 250 Hz, each trace spans 10 seconds. The singleton axis is a storage/channel wrapper, not an ECG lead. Lead order is explicitly:
[I,II,III,aVR,aVL,aVF,V_1,V_2,V_3,V_4,V_5,V_6].
The waveforms are stored as float64 after official per-lead clipping and train-set z-scoring. Evaluation inverts that affine transform back to clipped microvolts before reconstruction inference. This is a critical domain-transfer detail because PTB-XL models expect 500 Hz, 5,000-sample, physical-mV inputs with no per-record normalization. Resampling, unit conversion, axis ordering, and inverse normalization must all be validated independently.
Only the EchoNext test waveform array is present under the local data/echonext/ tree. Train, validation, and no_split waveform distributions therefore cannot be compared from this repository snapshot; their metadata are auditable, but claiming split-wise waveform parity would exceed the available artifact.
The 100,000-row metadata split is 72,475 train, 4,626 validation, 5,442 test, and 17,457 marked no_split. The unsplit records must not be silently added to training: their role is undefined by the local split field. The cohort is 53,581 male and 46,419 female records, with age 18–90 years (median 63; mean 61.18). Acquisition settings are heavily clinical—48,162 inpatient and 31,453 emergency records, compared with 17,194 outpatient and 3,191 procedural records—so this is not a consumer-wearable population sample.
Race/ethnicity counts are 31,013 Hispanic, 29,211 White, 16,461 Black, 3,428 Asian, 7,429 other, and 12,458 unknown. These are record counts rather than unique-patient counts and should not be presented as independent population denominators when patients have repeated ECGs.

text:
18.4 Endpoint prevalence and effective difficulty
The EchoNext classifier evaluates 12 echo-derived structural-heart-disease endpoints on the same 5,442 test records. Prevalence ranges from 0.37% (20 pulmonary-regurgitation positives) to 42.59% (2,318 composite SHD positives). Consequently:

accuracy is misleading for rare endpoints;
AUROC can look respectable while precision remains low;
average precision must be interpreted against prevalence;
F1 at a fixed 0.5 threshold mixes discrimination with calibration and threshold transport;
confidence intervals for the rarest endpoints will be wide even with 5,442 records.

18.4.1 Endpoint burden and co-occurrence
Structural-heart-disease endpoints overlap by construction: the composite label is positive when one or more component thresholds are met. Co-occurrence matters for macro metrics and error analysis because one ECG can contribute to multiple tasks. This block computes the test-set label-burden distribution and pairwise Jaccard overlap directly from the metadata.


Code
endpoint_columns = [
    column for column in echo.columns
    if column.endswith("_flag")
]
component_columns = [
    column for column in endpoint_columns
    if column != "shd_moderate_or_greater_flag"
]
echo_test = echo.loc[echo.split == "test"].copy()
labels = echo_test[component_columns].fillna(0).astype(bool)
burden = labels.sum(axis=1)
burden_table = (
    burden.value_counts().sort_index()
          .rename_axis("positive_component_labels")
          .reset_index(name="records")
)

cooccurrence = []
for i, left in enumerate(component_columns):
    for right in component_columns[i + 1:]:
        intersection = int((labels[left] & labels[right]).sum())
        union = int((labels[left] | labels[right]).sum())
        cooccurrence.append({
            "endpoint_a": left.removesuffix("_flag"),
            "endpoint_b": right.removesuffix("_flag"),
            "both_positive": intersection,
            "jaccard": intersection / union if union else np.nan,
        })
print("Number of positive component endpoints per test ECG")
display(burden_table)
pd.DataFrame(cooccurrence).sort_values(
    ["jaccard", "both_positive"], ascending=False
).head(20)

text:
18.5 Per-dataset waveform UMAP atlas
The repository reference manual at external/dataset_info.md enumerates seven clinical signal cohorts plus wearable/noise stress streams. This executable atlas reconciles that document with the files physically available at render time. It includes PTB-XL, EchoNext, LUDB, ISP, Sunnybrook, Zhejiang, and RDB. NSTDB/Fitbit stress streams are not plotted as an eighth clinical-cohort UMAP: they are perturbation sources, and no independently versioned raw stress corpus is present beneath the checkout’s data/ entry. Treating generated SNR variants as independent patients would inflate the apparent sample size.
Some statements in the reference manual are stronger than the locally verifiable evidence. In particular, the current data/rdb/ entry is empty, so RDB is read from the generation-bound waveform/delineation cache; ISP provenance and class semantics remain unresolved by the files themselves; and Zhejiang’s geographic/demographic description is not encoded in its arrays. The plots use those datasets, but their legends and interpretations remain inside the local evidence boundary.

18.5.1 Shared feature and sampling contract
Each ECG is mapped to the same 96-dimensional vector: for every canonical lead, RMS amplitude, interquartile range, 1st-to-99th percentile range, derivative RMS, and four relative Fourier-energy quartiles. Features are robust-scaled within each dataset. This representation is deliberately transparent and is not a learned ECG-AIM latent representation. Because sampling rates and units differ—and Zhejiang’s units/rate are not independently documented in its local tree—no pooled cross-dataset UMAP is used to claim domain similarity.
Sampling is deterministic and bounded. Small cohorts use all available records; larger cohorts use a SHA-256-ranked sample that is invariant to directory order. Raw signals are reduced one record at a time and are never copied into the HTML. RDB acquisition identifiers are replaced with one-way, namespace-scoped display tokens before plotting.

The diagnostics are part of the result, not decoration. Trustworthiness at k=5 measures whether local neighborhoods in the robust-scaled feature space survive projection. The stability column compares all pairwise distances from the seed-42 map with seeds 7 and 101 using Spearman rank correlation; it is rotation/reflection invariant. Low values invalidate visual cluster claims.
Panel B in every curated figure is the main protection against an attractive but misleading projection. It compares same-group nearest-neighbor frequency in the original 96-dimensional space, in the two-dimensional UMAP, and under the observed group imbalance. If the UMAP bar rises far above the original-space bar, the projection has visually amplified grouping. Panel C returns to a raw, purpose-linked measurement rather than asking UMAP to carry the claim.


18.5.2 PTB-XL — development-cohort support and split transport
PTB-XL is the reconstruction development cohort: 21,799 ten-second, 12-lead records in paired 500 Hz and 100 Hz releases. Official folds define training (1–8), validation (9), and holdout test (10); the patient-overlap audit above is the relevant independence gate. Diagnostic SCP labels and clinical metadata support reconstruction, morphology, and downstream diagnostic-retention work.
The curated question is not whether diagnoses form attractive clusters. It is whether official splits occupy comparable broad waveform support. Panel C shows global RMS by split; a split-specific island plus shifted RMS would trigger a device/site/quality investigation before interpreting model generalization.
