PTB-XL split support: waveform-feature UMAP, original-space projection check, and global RMS by official split.






18.5.3 EchoNext — structural-heart-disease phenotype
EchoNext contains 100,000 ECG–echocardiogram pairs, but only the 5,442-record official test waveform array is locally retained. Signals are 250 Hz and stored after released clipping and train-set normalization; the earlier audit reverses that affine transform for physical interpretation. Twelve echo-derived endpoints make this a transport and downstream-task cohort, not extra PTB-XL reconstruction training data.
The figure asks whether the released composite SHD endpoint aligns with broad ECG phenotype while showing LVEF outside the embedding. Visible separation is hypothesis generating: spectrum, care setting, age, and endpoint co-occurrence remain potential explanations.


Code
echo_diag = dataset_umap_diagnostics.set_index("dataset").loc["EchoNext"]
echo_fig = curated_figure("EchoNext", dataset_umaps["EchoNext"], echo_diag)
display(echo_fig); plt.close(echo_fig)





EchoNext structural phenotype: composite-SHD coloring, projection check, and LVEF distribution.






18.5.4 LUDB — expert morphology and atrial-fibrillation contrast
LUDB contributes 200 ten-second, 500 Hz, 12-lead ECGs with independently cardiologist-annotated P, QRS, and T boundaries on every lead. It is a morphology/delineation benchmark. Header diagnoses overlap and are not one mutually exclusive disease target.
AF is used as a narrow contrast because organized P-wave behavior is relevant to delineation. The 15 AF records are compared with the heterogeneous remainder, and age is shown explicitly as a basic confounding axis. This is not an estimate of AF diagnostic performance.

display(ludb_fig); plt.close(ludb_fig)





LUDB morphology: AF header contrast, projection check, and age distribution.






18.5.5 ISP — delineation split-shift audit under unresolved provenance
The local ISP package contains 403 training and 72 test records linked to 12-channel WFDB signals and serialized interval targets. Headers declare 1,000 Hz and the nonstandard unit token mkv. Although the reference manual assigns P/QRS/T semantics and a multicenter origin, no citation, license, source ID, or authoritative class dictionary is present locally. Those claims remain provisional here.
The defensible question is whether the provided test split shifts relative to training in waveform features or interval burden. Patient independence remains unverified, so split mixing cannot certify leakage freedom.

display(isp_fig); plt.close(isp_fig)





ISP split shift: train/test waveform UMAP, projection check, and interval burden.






18.5.6 Sunnybrook — physical-acquisition quality control
Sunnybrook is a 20-record local Philips XML transfer set with owner metadata and 179 machine-extracted features. The production decoder verifies sampling rate, lead order, resolution, and the centered ten-second crop. Cohort selection, subject multiplicity, adjudication, distribution authority, and the stronger “fully measured gold standard” claim are not independently established locally.
With 20 records, a disease-cluster UMAP would be especially unstable. This figure marks the two records whose maximum absolute amplitude exceeds 5 mV and shows the raw maxima. Its purpose is retained-transient and influence analysis, not prevalence generalization.

Sunnybrook quality control: amplitude-outlier UMAP, projection check, and per-record peak amplitude.






18.5.7 Zhejiang — dense-mask burden and waveform phenotype
The Zhejiang tree contains 334 record-level masks and 4,008 lead files (12 per record), each 20,000 samples long. Local arrays establish signal–mask pairing and the observed 0/1/2/3 mask convention. They do not independently establish institution, ethnicity, units, sampling rate, patient independence, or clinical diagnoses; those fields require external provenance.
The embedding is colored by QRS-mask-coverage quartile and Panel C exposes the underlying percentage. This tests whether gross segmentation burden tracks waveform phenotype; it does not turn a derived quartile into a clinical class.

Zhejiang dense masks: QRS-coverage UMAP, projection check, and raw QRS-mask fraction.






18.5.8 RDB — rhythm-diverse delineation and P-wave absence
RDB supplies 2,399 ten-second, 500 Hz, 12-lead records spanning eight canonical rhythm groups with lead-specific and consensus P/QRS/T intervals. The raw data/rdb/ entry is empty in this checkout, so this figure reads the generation-bound cache built from the raw CSV/annotation package. Cache records are source-bound, while public display labels are pseudonymized.
The figure asks whether rhythm diversity corresponds to broad waveform regimes and shows P-mask coverage by rhythm. This is directly relevant to AF hallucination: a model should not invent organized P waves when the reference mask supports their absence. Rhythm separation itself is not reconstruction quality.

The reference manual describes electrode motion, baseline wander, muscle artifact, and wearable-motion streams across calibrated SNR levels. No versioned raw NSTDB/Fitbit corpus is present beneath the local data/ entry, so this chapter does not invent a noise UMAP or repeat patients at several SNRs as if independent. 18.5.10 Cross-figure interpretation and falsification rules
For each panel, the only admissible first-pass question is whether its displayed group is locally mixed or separated in this specified feature representation. Separation does not prove diagnosis, site, physiology, or model learnability. PTB-XL and ISP colors are split diagnostics; EchoNext and RDB use released labels; LUDB uses a header-text AF indicator; Sunnybrook and Zhejiang colors are explicitly derived QC strata rather than clinical ground truth.
A visual finding is worth following only when trustworthiness and seed stability are adequate. The next test must operate in the original 96-dimensional feature space—for example, patient-grouped classification or a prespecified two-sample test with multiplicity control. Repeating UMAP until an attractive separation appears is not a valid analysis.

title: 18  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
text:
18.6 Signal-level EDA: what to measure

18.6.1 1. Units and inverse normalization
For each lead \ell, recover clipped microvolts using
x_{\mu V,\ell}=z_\ell\sigma_\ell+\mu_\ell.
Then convert once to millivolts if the reconstruction model expects mV:
x_{mV,\ell}=10^{-3}x_{\mu V,\ell}.
A thousand-fold unit error can produce finite tensors and plausible-looking normalized plots while destroying inference. Unit tests should assert known percentile ranges before and after conversion.


18.6.2 2. Clipping occupancy
Compute the fraction of values equal, or numerically close, to each provenance bound by lead. High occupancy indicates censored amplitude tails. Report this because peak-amplitude and ST-deviation errors are then conditional on the released clipping policy.
The rendered audit below reads a deterministic 256-record sample from the memory-mapped array, reverses the released affine normalization using PROVENANCE.json, and recomputes signal-validity and lead-law summaries. The compact disk does not retain a hash-bound full-array clipping audit, so this chapter does not present hard-coded full-array percentiles or occupancies as current evidence.


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(20260731)
echo_idx = np.sort(rng.choice(wave.shape[0], size=256, replace=False))

means = np.asarray(provenance["normalization"]["mean"], dtype=float)

    "aVL-(I-II/2)": echo_uv[:, :, 4] - (echo_uv[:, :, 0] - echo_uv[:, :, 1] / 2),
    "aVF-(II-I/2)": echo_uv[:, :, 5] - (echo_uv[:, :, 1] - echo_uv[:, :, 0] / 2),

Full-array clipping occupancy is a required future retained artifact. It must be computed in chunks, bound to the waveform/provenance hashes, and loaded here rather than transcribed into prose.


18.6.3 3. Lead-law residuals
The limb leads obey approximate linear relations:
III \approx II-I,\quad aVR \approx-\frac{I+II}{2},\quad
aVL \approx I-\frac{II}{2},\quad aVF \approx II-\frac{I}{2}.
Residual distributions detect lead permutations, polarity errors, scaling inconsistencies, and corrupted records. These are pipeline diagnostics, not targets to “repair” after looking at test performance.
The executable sample above supplies a regression diagnostic for the current local tensor. Full-array median and tail tolerances remain unreported until a hash-bound audit artifact is retained; sample estimates must not be promoted to full-cohort thresholds.


18.6.4 4. Spectral and morphology distributions
Report per-lead power in prespecified bands (baseline, P/T, QRS, high-frequency), R-peak count, RR variability, QRS width, QT/QTc, peak amplitude, and flatline fraction. Compare distributions before and after resampling. A global Pearson score can conceal loss of high-frequency QRS energy or systematic ST smoothing.


18.6.5 5. Cross-lead dependence
Plot the 12\times12 lead correlation matrix and the distribution of record-level condition numbers. Reconstruction difficulty depends on how much missing-lead information is identifiable from observed leads I, II, and V_2 (indices 0, 1, 7 in the locked registry). Strong average correlation does not imply that diagnostically important residual variation is recoverable.

title: 18  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
text:
18.7 Deep reconstruction diagnostics
A useful diagnostic stack separates four questions.








Layer
Question
Minimum outputs




Sample fidelity
Are point amplitudes close?
MAE/MSE, bias, Bland–Altman, peak error


Shape fidelity
Are morphology and timing preserved?
Pearson, derivative error, DTW, delineation deltas


Physiologic consistency
Do leads form a coherent ECG?
Einthoven residuals, VCG trajectory error, interval consistency


Diagnostic utility
Does a frozen model retain predictions?
per-task AUROC/AP/F1, calibration, paired probability drift



Failure analysis should be record based, not figure based. Rank records separately by MSE, missing-lead Pearson, QRS error, ST error, classifier probability drift, and signal-quality score. The intersection and disagreement among those lists reveal different failure modes:

low MSE + poor classifier fidelity: small but task-aligned feature loss;
high MSE + stable classifier output: nuisance amplitude or baseline mismatch;
strong global Pearson + poor QRS correlation: localized depolarization failure;
good morphology + lead-law violation: cross-lead incoherence;
good mean performance + subgroup tail failure: deployment inequity.

title: 18  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
section: 18.8 Statistical design for the factorial benchmark
text:
18.8 Statistical design for the factorial benchmark
The registered experiment is a 3\times2^4 grid, but primary factorial inference is the MSE-on 3\times2^3 subset. Eight MultiScale-VAE MSE-toggle cells are quarantined because paired checkpoints were tensor-identical under a historical decoder-loss defect. The complete 48-row table is useful for identity and forensics; it is not a uniformly valid four-factor inferential grid.
Use paired patient-cluster BCa intervals because all cells predict the same test patients and some patients contribute multiple records. For each family and endpoint, estimate
\Delta_k=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid k=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid k=0]
and prespecified two-way interactions. Family-wise morphology tests use the repository’s corrected threshold; exploratory downstream endpoints must be labeled exploratory. The existing results show significant QRS and ST improvements for full-versus-base in all three architecture families, while ECGFounder AUROC changes are not significant. That supports improved morphology without detected diagnostic-utility loss; it is not proof of clinical equivalence.

title: 18  Real-Cohort EDA, Integrity Checks, and Deep Diagnostics
text:
18.9 Reproducible audit checklist

Record exact file hashes and waveform shapes.
Assert patient-disjoint splits and stable record order.
Validate axis order, lead order, sampling rate, unit, and duration.
Quantify invalid demographics and structured missingness.
Report endpoint support before any classifier metric.
Preserve rare-task uncertainty; do not hide it in macro averages.
Compare pre/post-resampling spectra and intervals.
Inspect clipping occupancy and lead-law residuals.
Use patient-clustered paired inference.
Publish per-record outputs so tail failures remain inspectable.

title: 19  Dataset Atlas: LUDB, ISP, and Sunnybrook
text:
19.1 Provenance and governance ledger
LUDB, ISP, and Sunnybrook are complementary, not interchangeable. LUDB supplies dense lead-specific morphology annotations; ISP supplies interval targets for delineation; Sunnybrook supplies a small external set of fully measured clinical ECGs. A pooled “multi-dataset score” would erase those distinctions.
The local files do not all have the same documentation status. LUDB is the public PhysioNet release v1.0.1, cited as Kalyakulina et al. with DOI 10.13026/eegm-h675, and is distributed under the Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0. Its source states that 200 ten-second ECGs were collected in 2017–2018, annotated by cardiologists, with written consent and institutional review approval. EchoNext is a restricted PhysioNet resource; local provenance pins IntroECG commit 15233e… but does not attest which PhysioNet release version it corresponds to. The canonical dataset record and version history are available under DOI 10.13026/2j37-ba56.
The ISP folder in this repository does not include a citation, version, license, data-use terms, or a source identifier. Its three class meanings and sampling rate therefore remain unknown in this book. Sunnybrook has a local METADATA.json and README but no accompanying license, cohort selection protocol, subject identifiers, consent/ethics statement, or distribution authority. Until those fields are supplied by the data owner, Sunnybrook is a local exploratory transfer set and ISP is a locally present delineation artifact—not a fully provenance-resolved public benchmark.

19.1.1 Reproducible local fingerprints
The following fingerprints identify the exact artifacts read by this book. A tree hash includes each relative path, file size, and file digest, so a renamed, added, removed, or changed record alters the result.


Code
def file_sha256(path, chunk_size=8 * 1024 * 1024):
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as handle:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: handle.read(chunk_size), b""):
            digest.update(chunk)
    return digest.hexdigest()

def tree_sha256(root, patterns):
    files = sorted({
        path for pattern in patterns for path in root.rglob(pattern)
        if path.is_file()
    })
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    total_bytes = 0
    for path in files:
        size = path.stat().st_size
        total_bytes += size
        digest.update(str(path.relative_to(root)).encode())
        digest.update(str(size).encode())
        digest.update(file_sha256(path).encode())
    return len(files), total_bytes, digest.hexdigest()

fingerprints = []
for dataset, root, patterns in [
    ("LUDB", ROOT / "data/ludb", ["*.hea", "*.dat", "*.atr_*", "README", "LICENSE.txt"]),
    ("ISP", ROOT / "data/isp_delineation_dataset", ["*.hea", "*.dat", "*.csv"]),
    ("Sunnybrook", ROOT / "data/sunnybrook_12_lead_ecg_samples", ["*.xml", "*.csv", "*.json", "*.md"]),
]:
    n_files, n_bytes, digest = tree_sha256(root, patterns)
    fingerprints.append({
        "dataset": dataset, "resolved_root": str(root.resolve()),
        "files_hashed": n_files, "bytes_hashed": n_bytes, "sha256_tree": digest,
    })

for name in [
    "echonext_metadata_100k.csv", "EchoNext_test_waveforms.npy", "PROVENANCE.json"
]:
    path = ROOT / "data/echonext" / name
    fingerprints.append({
        "dataset": f"EchoNext: {name}",
        "resolved_root": str(path.resolve()), "files_hashed": 1,
        "bytes_hashed": path.stat().st_size, "sha256_tree": file_sha256(path),
    })

19.2.2 Demographics and diagnoses
The local headers yield 115 male and 85 female records. Age ranges from 11 to 90 years (mean 51.98, median 56). Diagnoses are overlapping free-text statements. Frequent statements include sinus rhythm (143), left ventricular hypertrophy (108), left atrial hypertrophy (102), normal electrical axis (75), left-axis deviation (66), incomplete right bundle-branch block (29), sinus bradycardia (25), and atrial fibrillation (15).

def parse_ludb_header(path):
    text = path.read_text()
    age = re.search(r"#<age>:\s*(\d+)", text)
    sex = re.search(r"#<sex>:\s*([MF])", text)
    statements = [
        line[1:].strip() for line in text.splitlines()
        if line.startswith("#") and not line.startswith("#<") and line[1:].strip()
    ]
    return {
        "age": int(age.group(1)) if age else np.nan,
        "sex": sex.group(1) if sex else "unknown",
        "statements": statements,
    }

19.2.5 Diagnostics LUDB enables
For P, QRS, and T waves, report onset, peak, and offset error by lead. Matching must be beat-aware and limited to a physiologic window; unconstrained nearest-neighbor matching can pair adjacent cycles. Minimum outputs are sensitivity, positive predictive value, median/IQR/95th-percentile timing error, cycle-mismatch rate, error versus wave amplitude, and interval consistency across leads.
A reconstruction can have high sample correlation but erase a low-amplitude P wave or shift its boundary enough to corrupt PR measurement. LUDB is designed to reveal precisely that failure.

19.3 ISP delineation targets

19.3.1 Local data contract
The ISP CSVs contain 403 training and 72 test rows. Each row includes file_name, age, binary sex coding, and a serialized list of (class, onset, offset) intervals. The training split contains 14,148 intervals and the test split 2,558.
Training class counts are 4,312 / 5,048 / 4,788 for classes 0/1/2; test counts are 793 / 900 / 865. Median widths are 116/110/182 samples in training and 114/110/182 in test. The ordering suggests P/QRS/T-like triplets, but the semantic mapping must come from source documentation rather than inference from sequence alone.
The WFDB files are present and link one-to-one to the CSV file_name inside each split. Their headers declare 12 channels, 1,000 samples/s, approximately 9,998–10,000 samples, and a nonstandard unit token mkv. The numerical scale is consistent with microvolt-like values, but the book does not silently relabel mkv as µV without authoritative provenance.

def load_isp(split):
    path = ROOT / "data/isp_delineation_dataset" / f"{split}_isp_delineation_data.csv"
    frame = pd.read_csv(path)
    frame["intervals"] = frame.target.map(ast.literal_eval)
    frame["interval_count"] = frame.intervals.map(len)
    return frame

isp_train = load_isp("train")
isp_test = load_isp("test")

def summarize_isp(frame, split):
    intervals = [x for row in frame.intervals for x in row]
    return {
        "split": split, "records": len(frame), "age_mean": frame.age.mean(),
        "age_sd": frame.age.std(), "sex_0": (frame.sex == 0).sum(),
        "sex_1": (frame.sex == 1).sum(), "intervals": len(intervals),
        "class_0": sum(x[0] == 0 for x in intervals),
        "class_1": sum(x[0] == 1 for x in intervals),
        "class_2": sum(x[0] == 2 for x in intervals),
    }

19.3.3 Interval integrity


Code
def interval_audit(frame, split):
    lengths = isp_headers.loc[
        isp_headers.split == split
    ].set_index("file_name").samples
    rows = []
    for _, record in frame.iterrows():
        xs = record.intervals
        record_length = int(lengths.loc[record.file_name])
        rows.append({
            "file_name": record.file_name,
            "valid_class": all(x[0] in {0, 1, 2} for x in xs),
            "positive_width": all(x[1] < x[2] for x in xs),
            "within_window": all(0 <= x[1] < x[2] <= record_length for x in xs),
            "sorted": all(xs[j][1] <= xs[j + 1][1] for j in range(len(xs) - 1)),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

isp_interval_integrity = pd.concat([
    interval_audit(isp_train, "train").assign(split="train"),
    interval_audit(isp_test, "test").assign(split="test"),
])
display(isp_interval_integrity.groupby("split").agg(
    records=("file_name", "count"),
    invalid_class=("valid_class", lambda x: (~x).sum()),
    invalid_width=("positive_width", lambda x: (~x).sum()),
    outside_window=("within_window", lambda x: (~x).sum()),
    unsorted=("sorted", lambda x: (~x).sum()),
))
invalid_isp = isp_interval_integrity.loc[
    ~(isp_interval_integrity.valid_class & isp_interval_integrity.positive_width & isp_interval_integrity.within_window & isp_interval_integrity.sorted)
]

The executed audit identifies invalid-width/out-of-window rows. Those records are quarantined from any benchmark or width summary until the source owner adjudicates whether the intervals should be clipped, corrected, or excluded. The descriptive counts above intentionally inventory the raw files and must not be mistaken for a cleaned training contract. The bounds come from each linked WFDB header; because source/version, class semantics, subject identity, and the unit token remain unresolved, no reconstruction checkpoint result or clinical timing claim is admissible on ISP yet.
Train and test ages have similar means (55.86 and 55.17), but test variability is larger (SD 19.16 versus 16.43). Sex coding 1 occurs in 153/403 training and 27/72 test rows. Similar marginals do not establish subject independence; file_name can restart within split directories.

The ranked table makes outlier selection algorithmic. ECG010 and ECG008 appear because of their decoded amplitudes, not because they were selected after viewing model performance. They remain in the primary descriptive analysis; robust medians and leave-one-record-out sensitivity should accompany means.
Fully measured limb leads make Sunnybrook valuable for detecting models that exploit algebraic limb-lead identities while failing on independently acquired morphology.


19.4.3 Hyperfeatures and evidence level
The Philips XLI pipeline supplies global heart rate, PR/QRS/QT/QTc and axes; per-lead P/Q/R/S/T amplitudes; P/QRS/T durations; ST onset/midpoint/J+80/end/slope; measured-lead flags; and diagnostic statements. These are machine-derived reference features, not cardiologist-adjudicated truth.
The set includes sinus rhythms, atrial fibrillation/flutter, old inferior MI, chamber/conduction findings, poor R-wave progression, and a mislaced-lead warning. With only 20 records, these are cases for external stress testing, not stable prevalence or broad clinical-effect estimation.


19.4.4 Retained transients and robust analysis
The comprehensive package retains a 20.44 mV V5 transient in ECG010 and a 6.66 mV V4 transient in ECG008 without clipping. Final analyses should report median/IQR and per-record influence alongside means, with an explicitly labeled sensitivity analysis excluding flagged transients. Silent removal would hide a real robustness failure.
Provenance also notes an approximately 18 µV physical Einthoven residual. This is an empirical acquisition reference, not a universal “errors below 18 µV are perfect” threshold: lead-law residual and reconstruction error are different quantities.
Sunnybrook superclass endpoints use non-adjudicated Philips statement proxies. ECGFounder has probability-fidelity evaluation only because compatible 150-task labels are absent. Those qualifications must appear beside every result table, not only in an appendix.

20.1 Why this chapter appears before model results
This chapter is an input-data audit, not evidence that one reconstruction loss is clinically superior. The local Zhejiang collection can support a useful external morphology benchmark, but the current result table contains only a ground-truth ceiling row. It therefore cannot yet estimate an MSE-versus-MMD contrast. Keeping that distinction visible prevents an available dataset from being mistaken for a completed experiment.
The audit below reads the files in data/zhejiang directly. It establishes what is physically present, checks signal-label pairing and mask integrity, and states the provenance information that is still missing. Later chapters may cite this cohort only within those bounds.

The table below is loaded rather than hard-coded. A ground-truth ceiling is a pipeline sanity check: applying the reference mask to itself should produce perfect overlap and zero boundary error. It is not a reconstruction-model result and supplies no loss-function comparison.

        c for c in current_results.columns

20.7 Interpretation boundary
The local files establish a paired 12-lead signal-and-mask corpus with internally consistent array structure. They do not, by themselves, establish cohort independence, diagnostic labels, RVOT/LVOT composition, sampling rate, voltage units, or licensing terms. Those facts require an authoritative README, paper, or data dictionary. Until model rows are generated under the protocol above, this chapter supports dataset readiness work—not a claim that MMD, MSE, or any other objective better preserves clinical morphology.

title: 21  PTB-XL Tensor, Lead, and Preprocessing Contract
text:
21.1 The contract actually used by training
The active reconstruction study reads precomputed PTB-XL tensors from data/ptb_xl/tensors/{train,val,test}. Each file is named by ECG record ID and contains a 12-by-5,000 floating-point array in canonical lead order. The model observes I, II, and V2—indices [0, 1, 7]—and reconstructs the nine remaining leads. Earlier text in this chapter incorrectly selected II, V1, and V5; that would define a different inverse problem and has been removed.
The content-pinned training contract declares 500 Hz, 10 seconds, mV, no normalization, train folds 1–8, validation fold 9, test fold 10, and batch size 1,024 for the running generation. “No normalization” and “no bandpass” mean the tensor values are passed to the model as stored; the Fourier/filter example later in this chapter is exploratory and is not a production transform.

title: 21  PTB-XL Tensor, Lead, and Preprocessing Contract
text:
21.2 Canonical lead geometry
The stored order is
[I,II,III,aVR,aVL,aVF,V1,V2,V3,V4,V5,V6].
The limb leads are linear combinations of three electrode potentials:
I=\Phi_{LA}-\Phi_{RA},\qquad II=\Phi_{LL}-\Phi_{RA},\qquad III=II-I,
aVR=-\frac{I+II}{2},\qquad aVL=I-\frac{II}{2},\qquad aVF=II-\frac{I}{2}.
These identities motivate cross-lead residual checks, but digitized clinical leads need not satisfy them to machine precision because of acquisition, filtering, quantization, timing, and export behavior. The precordial leads V1–V6 are separate chest-electrode measurements relative to a central terminal; they cannot be exactly derived from I and II.
The model observes I, II, and V2. The choice combines two limb views with one early precordial view; it is a study design choice, not a claim that this is the optimal sensor placement or that a smartwatch records all three.
crumbs: 21  PTB-XL Tensor, Lead, and Preprocessing Contract

title: 21  PTB-XL Tensor, Lead, and Preprocessing Contract
text:
21.3 Executable dataset loader
The loader below mirrors the active tensor semantics: numeric record ordering, weights_only=True, float conversion, shape validation, no signal normalization, and selection of [0,1,7]. Padding to 5,120 is performed in the U-Net training/evaluation path, not persisted in these tensor files.


Code
class PTBXLTensorDataset(Dataset):
    lead_names = ("I", "II", "III", "aVR", "aVL", "aVF", "V1", "V2", "V3", "V4", "V5", "V6")
    observed_indices = (0, 1, 7)

    def __init__(self, tensor_root, split):
        self.split = split
        self.files = sorted(
            (Path(tensor_root) / split).glob("*.pt"),
            key=lambda path: int(path.stem),
        )
        if not self.files:
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"No tensors found for split {split!r}")

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.files)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        path = self.files[index]
        target = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True).float()
        if tuple(target.shape) != (12, 5000):
            raise ValueError(f"Expected [12,5000] at {path}, got {tuple(target.shape)}")
        if not torch.isfinite(target).all():
            raise ValueError(f"Non-finite tensor at {path}")
        observed = target[list(self.observed_indices)]
        return observed, target, int(path.stem)

datasets = {split: PTBXLTensorDataset(TENSOR_ROOT, split) for split in ("train", "val", "test")}

21.5 Spectral audit of the stored signal
A periodogram is a record-level diagnostic, not proof of a universal “QRS band.” The example below uses Welch’s method on the named Lead I tensor. Spectral summaries depend on window, detrending, segment length, and any upstream acquisition filtering, so those choices remain visible.

lead_i = target[0].numpy()
frequencies, power = signal.welch(

21.6 Filtering demonstration—not the training transform
Zero-phase forward-backward filtering applies a causal filter in both directions, canceling net phase while squaring its magnitude response. It can still change peak amplitudes, boundary shapes, edge samples, and noise content. The comparison below is therefore a sensitivity illustration only. The content-pinned checkpoints were trained on the unfiltered stored tensors, and filtered signals must not be substituted at inference without a separately trained/evaluated contract.


Code
sos = signal.butter(3, [0.5, 45.0], btype="bandpass", fs=fs, output="sos")
filtered = signal.sosfiltfilt(sos, lead_i)
window = time_seconds < 3

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=time_seconds[window], y=lead_i[window], mode="lines",
    name="Stored Lead I (production tensor)", line=dict(width=1.3),
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=time_seconds[window], y=filtered[window], mode="lines",
    name="0.5–45 Hz demonstration", line=dict(width=1.3),
))
fig.update_layout(
    title=f"FILTER DEMONSTRATION — PTB-XL ECG {ecg_id}, not a training transform",
    xaxis_title="Time (s)", yaxis_title="mV", height=420,
)

title: 22  Implemented Reconstruction Architectures
text:
22.1 Two studies, two architecture scopes
This repository contains several generation-separated experiments. The locked 48-cell benchmark crosses three architecture families—MCMA-U-Net, WearECG MultiScale-VAE, and ECG-AIM—with 16 four-bit objective masks at seed 42. A historical 480-model plan holds MCMA-U-Net fixed across 160 seven-character masks and three seeds. The current seed-42 three-architecture seven-mask catalog instead contains 160 U-Nets, 155 MSVAEs, and 123 ECG-AIM checkpoints at the audited snapshot. One-lead ECG-AIM spatial and wavelet/SSL generations use a different input contract and are analyzed separately. ResNet and Conformer are not evaluated cells in these studies.
All families solve the same imputation task: observed leads I, II, and V2 (indices 0, 1, and 7 in the canonical order) condition reconstruction of a 12-lead, 5,000-sample array. Evaluation restores the three acquired leads exactly before computing all-lead endpoints; primary reconstruction endpoints are calculated on the nine missing leads so copied inputs cannot inflate performance.

from pathlib import Path

    with path.open("rb") as handle:

    raise FileNotFoundError("The generation-bound factorial-v4 registry and protocol audit are required; no cross-generation fallback is admissible.")

title: 22  Implemented Reconstruction Architectures
text:
22.2 Shared tensor and lead contract
Let the measured ECG be Y\in\mathbb{R}^{12\times T} in canonical order
[I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF, V1, V2, V3, V4, V5, V6].
With observed index set O=\{0,1,7\} and missing set M=\{0,\ldots,11\}\setminus O, a reconstructor f_\theta receives Y_O or an equivalent masked 12-lead representation and produces \tilde Y=f_\theta(Y_O). The evaluator applies the acquisition-preserving projection

\hat Y_j =
\begin{cases}
Y_j,&j\in O,\\
\tilde Y_j,&j\in M.
\end{cases}

This projection is important for deployment semantics—the device already measured Y_O—but it means all-lead metrics combine nine inferred channels with three exact channels. Missing-lead metrics on M are consequently the primary architecture-comparison endpoints.
The registry declares 500 Hz, 5,000 samples, mV, no normalization, and fixed train/validation/test inventories. Those fields are evaluation contracts, not defaults to infer for an external dataset. EchoNext, smartwatch, LUDB, ISP, Sunnybrook, and Zhejiang evaluations each require their own provenance and transformation audit.

title: 22  Implemented Reconstruction Architectures
text:
22.3 MCMA-U-Net: the historical 480-job study backbone
The implemented MCMAModel is an encoder-decoder with six channel widths
[16,32,64,128,256,512],
five stride-2 temporal reductions after an initial stride-1 block, five transposed-convolution upsampling stages, encoder-decoder concatenations, and a final 1\times1 projection to 12 output leads. Its residual-style down/up blocks use kernel size 13, GELU activation, GroupNorm, and InstanceNorm. This is not the generic three-level BatchNorm U-Net previously shown in this chapter; the executable source is scripts/train_mcma_3lead.py.
For a cross-correlation layer with kernel K, stride s, dilation d, and padding p,

L_{out}=\left\lfloor\frac{L_{in}+2p-d(K-1)-1}{s}+1\right\rfloor.

Five halvings require a length compatible with 2^5. The U-Net adapter pads a 5,000-sample record by 120 samples to 5,120, runs the network, then crops back to 5,000. Skip tensors are explicitly interpolated when a parity mismatch remains. The padding/cropping behavior is part of inference and must not be silently changed in another evaluator.


Code
import sys
import torch

if str(ROOT) not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from scripts.train_mcma_3lead import MCMAModel

unet = MCMAModel(in_channels=3, out_channels=12)
trainable = sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in unet.parameters() if parameter.requires_grad)
state_tensors = len(unet.state_dict())
source_path = ROOT / "scripts/train_mcma_3lead.py"

with torch.inference_mode():
    # A short length divisible by 32 verifies channel flow without allocating a
    # training-size activation graph. Production inference uses padded length 5120.
    probe_input = torch.zeros(1, 3, 320)
    probe_output = unet(probe_input)

    ("Input lead indices", "0, 1, 7"),
    ("Production input shape", "[batch, 3, 5120] after right padding"),
    ("Production output shape", "[batch, 12, 5000] after crop"),

title: 22  Implemented Reconstruction Architectures
text:
22.4 WearECG MultiScale-VAE
The locked registry declares a WearECG MultiScale-VAE with four latent channels and evaluation kind msvae. Its adapter constructs a 12-lead tensor in which unobserved channels are masked, passes explicit observed-lead indices, and calls the model’s imputation regressor when available. This family has a VAE base objective; factorial switches add auxiliary terms around that family-specific base. Its total objective scale is therefore not directly comparable to the U-Net total loss.
The loose primary checkpoints referenced by the locked registry are not present in the working checkpoint directory because the completed benchmark is distributed as a locked result bundle. This book reports the registry-declared architecture and artifact-backed evaluation outputs; it does not invent a parameter count by instantiating a possibly different local implementation.

title: 22  Implemented Reconstruction Architectures
text:
22.5 ECG-AIM
The locked registry declares ECG-AIM as an AliTok-style model with width 384, encoder depth 8, decoder depth 4, eight attention heads, and patch size 25. At 5,000 samples, patch size 25 corresponds to 200 temporal tokens before architecture-specific special tokens or masking. As with MultiScale-VAE, the evaluator supplies a masked 12-lead tensor and explicit lead indices, then obtains a 12-lead prediction through the registered adapter.
Attention width, depth, and token size describe computational structure; they do not by themselves imply better morphology or diagnostic fidelity. Those are measured in the paired PTB-XL and transfer endpoints. Cross-family rankings are descriptive because the backbone, base objective, optimizer schedule, and inductive bias all change together.

title: 22  Implemented Reconstruction Architectures
23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.1 Start with the executable contract
The seven-character design does not contain seven binary loss switches. Its mask is
m=m_{\mathrm{MSE}}m_{\mathrm{corr}}m_{\Delta}m_{\mathrm{VCG}}m_{\mathrm{ED}}m_{\mathrm{lead}}k_{\mathrm{MMD}},
where the first six positions are Boolean in the implementation and the last position is categorical: 0=none, 1=global adaptive RBF, 2=anatomical Laplacian, 3=anatomical multiscale IMQ, and 4=temporal K-means multiscale IMQ. The historical 480-job manifest fixes MSE on, crosses the other five Boolean terms with the five MMD levels, and repeats the resulting 2^5\times5=160 cells at three seeds. Current seed-42 architecture catalogs are reported separately and must not be mistaken for completion of that three-seed manifest.
This chapter describes scripts/common_loss.py exactly. It replaces a prior pedagogical loss class whose derivative norm, VCG transform, energy term, weights, and kernel choices did not match training.

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.2 Composite accumulation and scope
For active set A(m), training minimizes

\mathcal L_m(\hat Y,Y)=\sum_{j\in A(m)}\frac{\lambda_j}{s_j}\mathcal L_j(\hat Y,Y),

with the coefficients shown above. These are scale normalizers chosen to keep heterogeneous raw terms in a usable optimization range; they are not probabilistic calibration constants. Consequently, total losses from different masks are not directly comparable as prediction-quality scores.
The trainer computes these terms on the model’s full 12-lead output and full 12-lead target. It does not restrict the training objective to the nine missing leads and does not copy the three acquired leads before loss calculation. Evaluation later restores I, II, and V2 exactly for acquisition-consistent all-lead endpoints and reports missing-lead endpoints separately. This train/evaluation distinction must remain explicit.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.3 MSE and conditional-mean behavior
For N=BCT scalar entries,

\mathcal L_{\mathrm{MSE}}=\frac1N\sum_{b,c,t}(\hat y_{bct}-y_{bct})^2.

At the population-risk optimum, squared loss estimates the conditional expectation \mathbb E[Y\mid X]. When the missing leads are not uniquely determined by the observed leads, this can average plausible outcomes. That theorem does not say every finite trained MSE model returns a temporal or cohort-wide mean, nor does it prove peak attenuation in this dataset. Amplitude slopes, tail errors, and paired morphology measurements are needed to test the empirical hypothesis.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.4 Pearson loss with degenerate-signal handling
For each record and lead, the code centers over time and computes

r_{bc}=\frac{\sum_t(\hat y_{bct}-\bar{\hat y}_{bc})(y_{bct}-\bar y_{bc})}
{\sqrt{\max(V^{\hat y}_{bc},10^{-8})\max(V^y_{bc},10^{-8})}},
\qquad \mathcal L_{\mathrm{corr}}=1-\frac1{BC}\sum_{b,c}r_{bc}.

When either un-clamped variance is below 10^{-8}, the implementation assigns correlation zero for that lead-record pair. This avoids infinite gradients on flat signals. Pearson is invariant to positive affine rescaling and therefore cannot establish amplitude agreement by itself.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.5 First-difference loss
The active composite uses L1 distance between adjacent-sample differences:

\mathcal L_{\Delta}=\frac1{BC(T-1)}
\sum_{b,c,t}\left| (\hat y_{bc,t+1}-\hat y_{bct})-(y_{bc,t+1}-y_{bct})\right|.

common_loss.py also defines a squared derivative helper, but CombinatorialCompositeLoss calls derivative_l1_loss; the L1 equation is the study estimand. A first difference weights rapid sample-to-sample changes more strongly than slowly varying offsets, but preservation of a named QRS boundary remains an evaluation question.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.6 Kors vectorcardiogram loss
The implementation selects eight independent leads in order
[V1,V2,V3,V4,V5,V6,I,II]
and maps them to [X,Y,Z] with

K=\begin{bmatrix}
-0.130&0.050&-0.010&0.140&0.260&0.110&0.380&-0.070\\
0.060&-0.020&-0.050&0.060&0.170&0.130&-0.070&0.930\\
-0.430&-0.060&-0.040&-0.050&-0.080&-0.090&0.110&-0.230
\end{bmatrix}.

At each time sample, the loss is the mean cosine distance between predicted and target VCG vectors plus the L1 difference in their Euclidean magnitudes:

\mathcal L_{\mathrm{VCG}}=
\mathbb E_{b,t}[1-\cos(\hat v_{bt},v_{bt})]
+\mathbb E_{b,t}[|\|\hat v_{bt}\|_2-\|v_{bt}\|_2|].

This is not the 3-by-12 matrix or pure projected MSE previously printed in the book. It encodes a chosen inverse transform and should be interpreted as a spatial regularizer, not direct measurement of cardiac dipole ground truth.
The current cosine implementation is not identity-safe at zero norm: two zero VCG vectors incur an angle penalty rather than zero loss. The trainer also pads 5,000 samples to 5,120 with a zero target tail, so VCG-active cells receive an irreducible padded-tail contribution. VCG-active mixed-level cells are therefore implementation-under-audit and inadmissible for spatial-loss claims until valid-norm and padding masks are implemented and those cells are retrained.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.8 Limb-lead consistency
The lead term averages four MSE residuals:

\begin{aligned}
III&=II-I,\\
aVR&=-(I+II)/2,\\
aVL&=I-II/2,\\
aVF&=II-I/2.
\end{aligned}

It evaluates internal algebraic coherence of the predicted limb leads. Digitized targets can deviate from exact identities, so reducing the predicted residual does not automatically reduce target error; both reconstruction error and measured-target lead-law residuals must be reported.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.9 MMD level 1: global adaptive RBF
Each record is flattened across 12 leads and time. Squared Euclidean distances are divided by feature count, and the detached median of positive within-prediction, within-target, and cross distances supplies a batch-adaptive base bandwidth h. With multipliers a\in\{0.5,1,2,4\},

k_a(x,y)=\exp\left[-\frac{\|x-y\|_2^2/D}{2ah}\right],

and the code averages biased empirical MMD estimates (diagonal self-kernels included) across the four widths. Distance and kernel arithmetic are forced to float32 under mixed precision. Adaptation prevents the fixed-bandwidth underflow that affected a legacy high-dimensional implementation, but it also makes the kernel scale batch-dependent.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.10 MMD levels 2–3: overlapping anatomical blocks
The blocks are inferior [II, III, aVF], anteroseptal [V1–V4], lateral [I, aVL, V5, V6], all limb leads, and all precordial leads. Leads intentionally overlap across blocks. Each block is flattened per record, its MMD is divided by the number of leads in that block, and the five normalized block values are averaged.

Level 2 uses a Laplacian kernel \exp(-\|x-y\|_2/h) with target within-batch median distance.
Level 3 uses a four-width inverse-multiquadratic kernel (\|x-y\|_2^2+c^2)^{-1/2}. In the current implementation, however, the helper derives its scale from its second argument separately for the prediction–prediction, target–target, and cross terms. Those three terms therefore do not yet share one fixed kernel. Until a shared detached bandwidth is implemented and identity, symmetry, and non-negativity tests pass, this branch is reported as an implementation-under-audit rather than interpreted as a standard MMD estimand.

Because block weights, overlap, and bandwidth estimation are part of the estimand, “anatomical MMD” is not interchangeable with a generic per-lead MMD.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.11 MMD level 4: batch-dependent temporal K-means
For each training batch, the target is averaged over records, leaving one 12-dimensional vector per time sample. Four centroids are initialized from randomly selected time indices and updated for five Lloyd iterations. Time samples are assigned by 12-lead morphology, not constrained temporal adjacency. The resulting sets can be non-contiguous and should not be called detected P/QRS/T phases without validation.
For each cluster, predicted and target values are flattened over its time samples and all 12 leads, and the same IMQ helper used by level 3 is applied. It therefore inherits the unequal-kernel-scale defect described above and can be asymmetric under argument exchange. The four cluster losses are divided by four; empty clusters contribute zero through that fixed denominator. The training seed controls PyTorch random initialization, but cluster assignments remain batch-composition dependent. Level 4 is implementation-under-audit and inadmissible for MMD claims until one detached bandwidth per cluster is reused for all three kernel terms and affected cells are retrained.
crumbs: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design

title: 23  Implemented Loss Functions and Mixed-Level Design
text:
23.12 Executable component-scale diagnostic
The following deterministic probe loads an actual PTB-XL training batch, creates a stipulated attenuated/noisy prediction, and evaluates raw and weighted terms through the real implementation. It tests the software interface and illustrates scale only; the perturbation is not a trained model and the bars are not empirical loss effects.


Code
import torch
import plotly.express as px

torch.manual_seed(20260801)
files = sorted((ROOT / "data/ptb_xl/tensors/train").glob("*.pt"), key=lambda path: int(path.stem))[:8]
target = torch.stack([
    torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True).float() for path in files
])
prediction = 0.9 * target + 0.01 * torch.randn_like(target)

probe = CombinatorialCompositeLoss("1111111")

23.13 Interpretation rules

A lower total objective across two masks is not a fair performance comparison because the active terms and scale differ.
MMD and energy distance are batch-distribution estimators; batch size 1,024 is part of the current model-generation contract even though it is encoded in queue commands rather than the compact contract JSON.
Full-12-lead training terms can reward reconstruction of already observed leads; primary evaluation must retain nine-missing-lead endpoints.
None of these regularizers guarantees clinical feature preservation. Their effects must be estimated from paired, checkpoint-bound records with detector failures and uncertainty retained.
The mask identifies an objective configuration only when joined to seed, exact source bundle, data content roots, optimizer regime, and checkpoint digest.

title: 24  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
text:
24.1 Mathematical Formulations of QTc Interval Correction
Waveform reconstruction evaluation must look beyond global signal similarity (L_2 distance or Pearson correlation) to measure localized morphological features that dictate downstream clinical interpretation.
This chapter details the mathematical formulations and algorithmic implementations for P-QRS-T feature delineation, QT/QTc interval calculation, and bipartite event matching.
The QT interval measures the total temporal duration of ventricular depolarization (QRS) and repolarization (T-wave). Because QT duration shortens as heart rate increases, clinical interpretation requires calculating the rate-corrected QT interval (QTc).
Let \mathrm{QT} be the uncorrected interval in seconds and \mathrm{RR} be the cardiac cycle length (R\text{-to-}R interval) in seconds:
\mathrm{RR} = \frac{60}{\mathrm{HR} \text{ (bpm)}}

title: 24  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
text:
24.1.1 1. Bazett Formula (1920)
\mathrm{QTc}_B = \frac{\mathrm{QT}}{\sqrt{\mathrm{RR}}}

Limitation: Derived empirically from a small cohort and can show residual heart-rate dependence. The fixed-QT illustration below is not evidence for a clinical heart-rate threshold or false-positive rate.



24.1.2 2. Fridericia Formula (1920)
\mathrm{QTc}_F = \frac{\mathrm{QT}}{\sqrt[3]{\mathrm{RR}}}

Use boundary: Fridericia is commonly used in drug-induced repolarization studies, but formula choice is protocol- and population-dependent; individualized correction may be preferable when justified. It is not presented here as a universal standard.



24.1.3 3. Framingham Linear Formula (1992)
\mathrm{QTc}_{\text{Fram}} = \mathrm{QT} + 0.154 \cdot (1 - \mathrm{RR})


24.1.4 4. Hodges Linear Formula (1983)
\mathrm{QTc}_{\text{Hodges}} = \mathrm{QT} + 0.00175 \cdot (\mathrm{HR} - 60)

title: 24  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
section: 24.2 Bipartite Event Matching & Fiducial Error Assignment
text:
24.2 Bipartite Event Matching & Fiducial Error Assignment
Evaluating delineation error requires pairing reference sample indices R = \{r_i\}_{i=1}^{N} with predicted sample indices P = \{p_j\}_{j=1}^{M}. For a prespecified endpoint tolerance of 50 ms, the sample-domain gate is \tau_s=0.050f_s samples; endpoint-specific sensitivity analyses are still required.

24.2.1 Bipartite Graph Optimization Problem
First maximize the cardinality of a one-to-one matching, then—among maximum-cardinality matchings—minimize total absolute timing error:
\max |M|,\qquad \min_{M:\,|M|=|M|_{\max}}\sum_{(i,j)\in M}|r_i-p_j|,
\quad |r_i-p_j|\le 0.050f_s.
Unmatched reference events r_i are categorized as False Negatives (FN); unmatched predicted events p_j are False Positives (FP).


24.2.2 Signed Timing Error Definition
For matched event pairs:
e_i = 1000 \cdot \frac{p_{\pi(i)} - r_i}{f_s} \quad \text{(in milliseconds, ms)}

e_i > 0: Reconstructed wave is delayed relative to ground truth (late detection).
e_i < 0: Reconstructed wave is advanced relative to ground truth (early detection).



24.2.3 QTc Formula Sensitivity Across Heart Rates (40-140 bpm)
Below, we plot algebraic fixed-QT sensitivity across 40–140 bpm. Holding QT at 400 ms cannot measure physiological correction accuracy or stability because observed QT normally varies with RR.


Code
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

hr_range = np.linspace(40, 140, 100)
rr_seconds = 60.0 / hr_range
qt_ms = 400.0  # Constant 400 ms QT interval

qtc_bazett = qt_ms / np.sqrt(rr_seconds)
qtc_fridericia = qt_ms / (rr_seconds ** (1/3))
qtc_framingham = qt_ms + 154.0 * (1.0 - rr_seconds)
qtc_hodges = qt_ms + 1.75 * (hr_range - 60.0)

fig_qtc = go.Figure()
fig_qtc.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=hr_range, y=qtc_bazett, mode='lines', line=dict(color='#f43f5e', width=2), name='Bazett (Overcorrects at High HR)'))
fig_qtc.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=hr_range, y=qtc_fridericia, mode='lines', line=dict(color='#38bdf8', width=2), name='Fridericia'))
fig_qtc.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=hr_range, y=qtc_framingham, mode='lines', line=dict(color='#10b981', width=2), name='Framingham Linear Correction'))
fig_qtc.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=hr_range, y=qtc_hodges, mode='lines', line=dict(color='#fbbf24', width=2), name='Hodges Linear Correction'))

fig_qtc.update_layout(
    title="QTc Correction Formula Heart Rate Sensitivity (Fixed 400 ms QT)",
    xaxis_title="Heart Rate (bpm)",
    yaxis_title="Corrected QTc (ms)",
    template="plotly_dark",

title: 24  Diagnostic Integrity & Clinical Delineation
text:
24.3 Didactic Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) Delineation
The following section explains one automated delineation approach. It is a synthetic software demonstration, not a result from a repository checkpoint and not a validation of the generation-bound temporal-MMD evaluator. That evaluator must separately disclose its detector, detection failures, and paired-beat coverage.
Continuous Wavelet Transforms (CWT) can use a Mexican Hat mother wavelet \psi(t) to detect steep wave zero-crossings:
\psi(t) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3\sigma} \pi^{1/4}} \left( 1 - \frac{t^2}{\sigma^2} \right) e^{-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}}
High-resolution scales isolate sharp QRS spikes (10-25\text{ Hz}), while lower-resolution scales detect smooth P and T wave peaks (1-10\text{ Hz}).


Code
import neurokit2 as nk
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# 1. Simulate one 5-second ECG-like trace at 500 Hz
sampling_rate = 500
ecg_signal = nk.ecg_simulate(duration=5, sampling_rate=sampling_rate, heart_rate=72)

# 2. Clean signal using zero-phase Butterworth bandpass filter
ecg_cleaned = nk.ecg_clean(ecg_signal, sampling_rate=sampling_rate, method="neurokit")

# 3. Locate R-peaks
_, rpeaks = nk.ecg_peaks(ecg_cleaned, sampling_rate=sampling_rate)

# 4. Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) Delineation for P, Q, S, T boundaries
signals, waves = nk.ecg_delineate(ecg_cleaned, rpeaks, sampling_rate=sampling_rate, method="cwt")

# Generate time vector in seconds
t = np.linspace(0, len(ecg_cleaned) / sampling_rate, len(ecg_cleaned))

# Create Plotly Interactive Delineation Viewer
fig_del = go.Figure()

# Cleaned ECG trace
fig_del.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=t, y=ecg_cleaned, mode='lines', 
    name='Cleaned synthetic trace',
    line=dict(color='#38bdf8', width=2)
))

# Helper to plot fiducial markers
def add_fiducial(indices, color, symbol, name):
    valid_idx = [int(i) for i in indices if not np.isnan(i)]
    if len(valid_idx) > 0:
        fig_del.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=t[valid_idx], y=ecg_cleaned[valid_idx],
            mode='markers', 
            marker=dict(color=color, size=9, symbol=symbol, line=dict(width=1, color='white')),
            name=name
        ))

# Add P, R, and T wave markers
add_fiducial(rpeaks['ECG_R_Peaks'], '#f43f5e', 'star', 'R-Peak')
add_fiducial(waves['ECG_P_Onsets'], '#a855f7', 'triangle-right', 'P-Onset')
add_fiducial(waves['ECG_P_Offsets'], '#a855f7', 'triangle-left', 'P-Offset')
add_fiducial(waves['ECG_T_Onsets'], '#10b981', 'triangle-right', 'T-Onset')
add_fiducial(waves['ECG_T_Offsets'], '#10b981', 'triangle-left', 'T-Offset')

fig_del.update_layout(
    title="DIDACTIC SIMULATION — Automated CWT Delineation",
    xaxis_title="Time (seconds)",
    yaxis_title="Simulated amplitude (arbitrary units)",
    template="plotly_dark",
    height=450, margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=40, b=20)

text:
24.4 QTc Formula Comparison Function


Code
def calculate_qtc_variations(qt_ms, rr_ms):
    """
    Computes QTc across Bazett, Fridericia, Framingham, and Hodges formulas.
    
    Args:
        qt_ms (float): Uncorrected QT interval in milliseconds.
        rr_ms (float): R-R interval in milliseconds.
    """
    qt_sec = qt_ms / 1000.0
    rr_sec = rr_ms / 1000.0
    hr = 60.0 / rr_sec
    
    qtc_bazett = (qt_sec / np.sqrt(rr_sec)) * 1000.0
    qtc_fridericia = (qt_sec / (rr_sec ** (1/3))) * 1000.0
    qtc_framingham = (qt_sec + 0.154 * (1.0 - rr_sec)) * 1000.0
    qtc_hodges = qt_ms + 1.75 * (hr - 60.0)
    
    return {
        "Heart Rate (bpm)": round(hr, 1),
        "Uncorrected QT (ms)": round(qt_ms, 1),
        "QTc Bazett (ms)": round(qtc_bazett, 1),
        "QTc Fridericia (ms)": round(qtc_fridericia, 1),
        "QTc Framingham (ms)": round(qtc_framingham, 1),
        "QTc Hodges (ms)": round(qtc_hodges, 1)
    }

# Compare QTc corrections at Normal HR (70 bpm) vs Tachycardia (110 bpm)
normal_hr_stats = calculate_qtc_variations(qt_ms=400, rr_ms=857) # 70 bpm
tachy_hr_stats = calculate_qtc_variations(qt_ms=340, rr_ms=545)  # 110 bpm

print("==================================================")
print("Normal Heart Rate (70 bpm) QTc Comparison:")
print(normal_hr_stats)
print("\nTachycardic Heart Rate (110 bpm) QTc Comparison:")
print(tachy_hr_stats)
print("==================================================")

title: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text:
25.1 Mathematical Proof: Why L_2 Minimization Induces Regression to the Mean
At the unrestricted population-risk optimum, squared-error regression returns the conditional mean E[Y\mid X]. This theorem motivates—but does not prove for a finite trained network—the hypothesis that ambiguous missing-lead structure may be attenuated. Peak amplitude, interval timing, morphology, and clinical classification therefore remain empirical endpoints; none follows automatically from the theorem.
This chapter presents the complete mathematical proof of L_2 variance shrinkage, followed by an advanced statistical battery using Bland-Altman Agreement Analysis.
crumbs: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean

title: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text:
25.1.1 Theorem 1: L_2 Minimization Yields the Conditional Expectation
Let X \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{in} \times T} be the input lead tensor and Y \in \mathbb{R}^{C_{out} \times T} be the target 12-lead tensor with joint probability density p(X, Y).
Objective: Find a neural network function f^*(X) minimizing the expected squared error:
f^*(X) = \arg\min_f \mathbb{E}_{(X, Y)} \left[ \| f(X) - Y \|_2^2 \right]
Proof: Using the law of total expectation, we expand the expected loss:
\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)} \left[ \| f(X) - Y \|_2^2 \right] = \mathbb{E}_{X} \left[ \mathbb{E}_{Y|X} \left[ \| f(X) - Y \|_2^2 \;\middle|\; X \right] \right]
To minimize the outer expectation, we minimize the inner conditional expectation point-wise for every fixed value of X = x:
\mathcal{L}(f(x)) = \int (f(x) - y)^2 \, p(y \mid x) \, dy
Differentiating \mathcal{L}(f(x)) with respect to f(x) and setting the derivative to zero:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial f(x)} = \int 2 \cdot (f(x) - y) \, p(y \mid x) \, dy = 0
2 \cdot f(x) \int p(y \mid x) \, dy - 2 \int y \cdot p(y \mid x) \, dy = 0
Since \int p(y \mid x) \, dy = 1:
f^*(x) = \int y \cdot p(y \mid x) \, dy = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]
\blacksquare



25.1.2 Corollary 1: Marginal variance of the conditional mean
By the Law of Total Variance:
\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\big) + \mathbb{E}\big[\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X)\big]
Since \operatorname{Var}(Y \mid X) \ge 0, it follows that:
\operatorname{Var}\big(f^*(X)\big) = \operatorname{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]\big) \le \operatorname{Var}(Y)
For a scalar coordinate, equality holds when the expected conditional variance is zero. For a waveform tensor, the corresponding statement is coordinatewise or in terms of the conditional covariance matrix. Whether a particular lead set leaves nonzero conditional uncertainty is a property of the data distribution and cannot be inferred merely from the number of observed leads.
This is a marginal-distribution statement about the population optimum. It does not imply that every finite L_2 model shrinks QRS peaks or flattens P/T waves. Those are prespecified hypotheses to test with paired record-level amplitude and delineation endpoints, detector-failure denominators, and patient-clustered uncertainty.



25.1.3 Wasserstein-1 Distance (W_1 Earth Mover’s Metric)
To quantify the total probability mass shift caused by variance shrinkage, we compute the 1D Wasserstein-1 Distance (W_1) between the empirical cumulative distribution functions F_P(u) (ground truth) and F_Q(u) (prediction):
W_1(P, Q) \triangleq \inf_{\gamma \in \Pi(P, Q)} \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \gamma} \left[ \|x - y\|_1 \right] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left| F_P(u) - F_Q(u) \right| \, du
where \Pi(P, Q) denotes the set of all joint distributions whose marginals are P and Q.

Physical Interpretation: W_1 measures the minimum “work” (probability mass \times transport distance) required to transform the predicted peak amplitude distribution Q into the true physiological distribution P.
Separate estimands: training with a finite-weight mini-batch MMD term does not guarantee that held-out W_1 is zero. MMD and W_1 must be measured separately under the registered evaluation protocol; any association between them is an empirical result.

title: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
section: 25.2 Why Pearson Correlation (r) Cannot Prove Agreement
text:
25.2 Why Pearson Correlation (r) Cannot Prove Agreement
A common misconception in model evaluation is using Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) to claim reconstruction accuracy. As proved by Giavarina (2015): - Pearson correlation measures linear association, not agreement. - If \hat{Y} = 0.5 \cdot Y + 0.1, the correlation is perfect (r = 1.0), yet the predicted amplitudes suffer a 50\% clinical loss!
To measure true clinical comparability, we must use Bland-Altman Agreement Analysis.
crumbs: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean

title: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text:
25.3 Advanced Bland-Altman Statistical Battery
The didactic battery below illustrates four agreement summaries or diagnostics; it is not four non-parametric hypothesis tests:

Mean Bias (\bar{d}): \bar{d} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i, \quad d_i = \hat{y}_i - y_i
95% Limits of Agreement (LoA): \text{LoA} = \left[ \bar{d} - 1.96 \cdot s_d, \;\; \bar{d} + 1.96 \cdot s_d \right], \quad s_d = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (d_i - \bar{d})^2}
Non-Parametric BCa Bootstrap Confidence Intervals (9,999 Resamples): Constructs 95% Confidence Intervals for \bar{d} without assuming Gaussian errors.
Levene’s Test as a limited diagnostic: Tests a grouped variance null; failure to reject does not verify homoscedasticity. A continuous difference-versus-mean model and residual visualization are needed for proportional-bias assessment.
crumbs: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean

title: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean
text:
25.4 Python Implementation: Bland-Altman Statistical Suite






WarningDemonstration inputs only



The code below deliberately stipulates 30% attenuation for one synthetic sample and 1% attenuation for another. Its numerical output is a software/statistics demonstration, not a measurement of any repository checkpoint.




Code
import torch
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from scipy import stats

def compute_ba_statistics(pred_peaks, target_peaks, model_name):
    """
    Computes Bland-Altman agreement statistics: Mean Bias, 95% LoA, 
    BCa Bootstrap 95% CI, Shapiro-Wilk Normality, and Levene Homoscedasticity.
    """
    diff = pred_peaks - target_peaks
    mean_val = (pred_peaks + target_peaks) / 2.0
    
    bias = np.mean(diff)
    std_diff = np.std(diff, ddof=1)
    
    loa_lower = bias - 1.96 * std_diff
    loa_upper = bias + 1.96 * std_diff
    
    # 1. Non-parametric BCa Bootstrap for Bias 95% CI (9,999 resamples)
    res = stats.bootstrap(
        (diff,), np.mean, 
        confidence_level=0.95, n_resamples=9999, method='BCa'
    )
    ci_lower, ci_upper = res.confidence_interval
    
    # 2. Shapiro-Wilk test for normality of differences
    stat_sw, p_value_sw = stats.shapiro(diff)
    normality_msg = "Normality not rejected" if p_value_sw > 0.05 else "Normality rejected"
    
    # 3. Levene's Test for Homoscedasticity (Lower half vs Upper half)
    median_val = np.median(mean_val)
    diff_lower = diff[mean_val <= median_val]
    diff_upper = diff[mean_val > median_val]
    stat_lev, p_value_lev = stats.levene(diff_lower, diff_upper)
    levene_msg = "Equal-variance null not rejected" if p_value_lev > 0.05 else "Equal-variance null rejected"
    
    # 4. Percentage bias calculation
    pct_diff = (diff / mean_val) * 100
    pct_bias = np.mean(pct_diff)
    
    print(f"=== {model_name} Bland-Altman Audit ===")
    print(f"Mean Bias (\u0304d): {bias:.4f} mV (BCa 95% CI: [{ci_lower:.4f}, {ci_upper:.4f}])")
    print(f"Limits of Agreement (95% LoA): [{loa_lower:.4f}, {loa_upper:.4f}]")
    print(f"Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test: p = {p_value_sw:.4f} ({normality_msg})")
    print(f"Levene Homoscedasticity Test: p = {p_value_lev:.4f} ({levene_msg})")
    print(f"Percentage Bias: {pct_bias:.2f}%")
    print("-" * 50)
    
    return mean_val, diff, bias, loa_lower, loa_upper, pct_diff, pct_bias

# Simulate N=300 peak amplitudes to demonstrate the statistical interface only
np.random.seed(42)
target_peaks = np.random.normal(1.2, 0.4, 300)

# 1. Stipulated MSE Model (30% amplitude attenuation factor)
mse_peaks = target_peaks * 0.70 + np.random.normal(0, 0.03 * np.abs(target_peaks), 300)

# 2. Stipulated Combinatorial Model (Preserves 99% peak amplitude)
comp_peaks = target_peaks * 0.99 + np.random.normal(0, 0.02, 300)

(mse_means, mse_diffs, mse_bias, mse_loa_l, mse_loa_u, mse_pct_diff, mse_pct_bias) = compute_ba_statistics(mse_peaks, target_peaks, "MSE Model ($L_2$)")
(comp_means, comp_diffs, comp_bias, comp_loa_l, comp_loa_u, comp_pct_diff, comp_pct_bias) = compute_ba_statistics(comp_peaks, target_peaks, "Combinatorial Loss Model")

Limits of Agreement (95% LoA): [-0.6038, -0.1173]

Levene Homoscedasticity Test: p = 0.4654 (Equal-variance null not rejected)

This simulation demonstrates how conditional-mean shrinkage would appear in Bland–Altman diagnostics under the stipulated attenuation factors. It does not prove that the trained MSE cells attenuate amplitudes, nor that a composite loss is required or sufficient for clinical fidelity. Those are empirical hypotheses tested with the paired, generation-bound artifacts.
crumbs: 25  Rigorous Agreement & The Mathematics of Regression to the Mean

title: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
text:
26.1 Signal Quality Index (SQI) Formulations
ECG reconstruction models intended for wearable or clinical use must be evaluated across patient subgroups and realistic signal degradation. This chapter formulates measurement interfaces; its executable waveform example is synthetic and does not report robustness or fairness for a trained checkpoint.
Signal Quality Indices (SQIs) evaluate whether a recorded or reconstructed ECG is suitable for clinical delineation without requiring ground-truth clean signals.
crumbs: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)

title: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
text:
26.1.1 1. Kurtosis SQI (kSQI)
Kurtosis measures the “peakedness” of the signal amplitude distribution:
kSQI = \frac{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^4}{\left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \right]^2}

Interpretation boundary: QRS complexes can increase kurtosis and Gaussian noise has population kurtosis 3, but fixed cutoffs such as 2 or 5 are not universal quality labels. Rhythm, lead, filtering, record length, and estimator convention can all change the value; thresholds require cohort-specific validation.



26.1.2 2. Skewness SQI (sSQI)
Skewness measures asymmetry around the mean:
sSQI = \frac{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^3}{\left[ \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \right]^{3/2}}


26.1.3 3. Relative QRS Power Spectral SQI (pSQI)
Measures the proportion of signal power concentrated within the QRS frequency band (5 - 15\text{ Hz}) relative to the total physiological band (5 - 40\text{ Hz}):
pSQI = \frac{\int_{5}^{15} P(f) \, df}{\int_{5}^{40} P(f) \, df}
where P(f) = |X(f)|^2 is the Power Spectral Density obtained via Fast Fourier Transform.
crumbs: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)

title: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
section: 26.2 Noise Stress Testing Mathematics & Noise Models
text:
26.2 Noise Stress Testing Mathematics & Noise Models
The executable teaching example implements the first two models below. The third is a protocol specification, not executable evidence in this chapter:
x_{\text{corrupted}}(t) = x(t) + n_{\text{artifact}}(t)

26.2.1 1. Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN)
Noise variance \sigma_n^2 is parameterized by target Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR in dB):
\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_{\text{signal}}}{P_{\text{noise}}} \right) \implies \sigma_n = \sqrt{\frac{P_{\text{signal}}}{10^{\text{SNR}_{\text{dB}} / 10}}}
where P_{\text{signal}} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} x(t)^2.


26.2.2 2. Respiratory Baseline Wander (n_{\text{BW}})
Simulates low-frequency chest impedance drift caused by respiration (0.1 - 0.5\text{ Hz}):
n_{\text{BW}}(t) = A_{\text{BW}} \cdot \sin(2\pi f_{\text{resp}} t + \phi)


26.2.3 3. Electromyographic (EMG) Muscle Tremor Noise (n_{\text{EMG}})
Modeled as a high-frequency filtered autoregressive process (> 35\text{ Hz}) simulating random muscle contractions.
Not implemented below. A reportable implementation must specify the filter, autoregressive parameters, lead covariance, random seed, and achieved finite-sample SNR.
crumbs: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)

title: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
text:
26.3 Subgroup Fairness & Disparity Metrics
When evaluating performance across demographic subgroups A \in \{\text{Male}, \text{Female}\} or age brackets A \in \{\text{Age} \le 65, \text{Age} > 65\}, reporting global aggregate metrics hides disparities.

26.3.1 1. Absolute Performance Disparity (\Delta_{\text{perf}})
\Delta_{\text{perf}} = \text{Metric}(A = \text{Group}_1) - \text{Metric}(A = \text{Group}_2)


26.3.2 2. Paired Reconstruction Degradation (\Delta_{\text{recon}})
Measures the change in metric induced specifically by model reconstruction:
\Delta_{\text{recon}}(A_g) = \text{Metric}\big(\hat{Y}_{A_g}\big) - \text{Metric}\big(Y_{A_g}\big)
\text{Fairness Disparity} = \Delta_{\text{recon}}(\text{Male}) - \Delta_{\text{recon}}(\text{Female})
Using patient-clustered non-parametric bootstrapping ensures that repeated recordings from the same patient do not artificially shrink confidence intervals.
crumbs: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)

title: 26  Fairness, Noise Robustness, and Signal Quality Index (SQI)
section: 26.4 Python Implementation: SQI Computation & Noise Stress Suite
text:
26.4 Python Implementation: SQI Computation & Noise Stress Suite


Code
import numpy as np
import scipy.signal as signal
from scipy import stats
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

def compute_sqi_metrics(ecg_signal, fs=500):
    """
    Calculates kSQI, sSQI, and pSQI for a 1D ECG signal.
    """
    # 1. Kurtosis SQI
    ksqi = stats.kurtosis(ecg_signal, fisher=False)
    
    # 2. Skewness SQI
    ssqi = stats.skew(ecg_signal)
    
    # 3. Power Spectrum SQI (pSQI)
    freqs, psd = signal.welch(ecg_signal, fs=fs, nperseg=fs)
    
    qrs_power = np.sum(psd[(freqs >= 5) & (freqs <= 15)])
    total_power = np.sum(psd[(freqs >= 5) & (freqs <= 40)]) + 1e-8
    psqi = qrs_power / total_power
    
    return {"kSQI": round(ksqi, 3), "sSQI": round(ssqi, 3), "pSQI": round(psqi, 3)}

def inject_noise_stress(ecg_signal, snr_db=12, noise_type="gaussian", fs=500, rng=None):
    """
    Injects synthetic AWGN or Baseline Wander at a target SNR in dB.
    """
    p_signal = np.mean(ecg_signal ** 2)
    t = np.linspace(0, len(ecg_signal) / fs, len(ecg_signal))
    
    rng = np.random.default_rng(20260801) if rng is None else rng
    if noise_type == "gaussian":
        p_noise = p_signal / (10 ** (snr_db / 10.0))
        noise = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(p_noise), len(ecg_signal))
    elif noise_type == "baseline_wander":
        # Respiratory drift at 0.3 Hz
        drift = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.3 * t)
        p_drift = np.mean(drift ** 2)
        scale = np.sqrt((p_signal / (10 ** (snr_db / 10.0))) / p_drift)
        noise = scale * drift
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown noise type: {noise_type}")
        
    return ecg_signal + noise

# Simulate a deterministic ECG-like teaching signal. This is not an acquired ECG.
fs = 500
t = np.linspace(0, 2.0, 1000)
clean_ecg = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1.2 * t) ** 21 + 0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1.2 * t + 0.8) ** 3

# Inject AWGN (12 dB) and Baseline Wander (6 dB)
rng = np.random.default_rng(20260801)
noisy_awgn = inject_noise_stress(clean_ecg, snr_db=12, noise_type="gaussian", fs=fs, rng=rng)
noisy_bw = inject_noise_stress(clean_ecg, snr_db=6, noise_type="baseline_wander", fs=fs, rng=rng)

# Compute SQI Metrics
sqi_clean = compute_sqi_metrics(clean_ecg, fs=fs)
sqi_awgn = compute_sqi_metrics(noisy_awgn, fs=fs)
sqi_bw = compute_sqi_metrics(noisy_bw, fs=fs)

print("==================================================")
print(f"Clean ECG SQI Metrics:     {sqi_clean}")
print(f"AWGN 12dB Corrupted SQI:    {sqi_awgn}")
print(f"Baseline Drift 6dB SQI:    {sqi_bw}")
print("==================================================")

title: 27  Generation-Bound 48-Cell Factorial Benchmark
text:
27.1 Artifact, identity, and completeness gate
This chapter reports the completed factorial_v4 generation: three architecture families crossed with sixteen four-bit objective masks at seed 42. It does not pool the separate 480-job mixed-level U-Net study, whose live protocol and completion gates appear in Chapter 12.
The identifier family__e?c?m?d?__s42 encodes pointwise MSE (E), correlation loss (C), repaired adaptive multiscale RBF MMD (M), and first-derivative loss (D). Primary confirmatory factorial inference is restricted to the MSE-on (2^3) design. The full MSE toggle is supplementary because a historical MultiScale-VAE decoder-loss defect made eight MSE-off/on checkpoint pairs identical; the quarantine is part of the artifact contract.

import plotly.express as px

def nondominated(group, x, y):
    values = group[[x, y]].to_numpy()
    return np.array([not np.any((values[:,0] >= a) & (values[:,1] >= b) &
                                ((values[:,0] > a) | (values[:,1] > b))) for a,b in values])

valid_master = master.loc[master.inference_status == "valid"].copy()

).sort_index()

title: 27  Generation-Bound 48-Cell Factorial Benchmark
text:
27.8 Quarantined supplementary MSE toggle
The 4-factor supplementary file remains available for forensics, but the MultiScale-VAE MSE toggle is excluded from claims because paired checkpoints were tensor-identical under the historical detached decoder-loss path. The prespecified MSE-on (2^3) effects and familywise full-versus-MSE-only endpoint tests are reported only according to the locked claim-scope rules. Rendering never rewrites the release report.

title: 27  Generation-Bound 48-Cell Factorial Benchmark
text:
27.9 Interpretation boundary
The defensible result is architecture- and endpoint-specific: auxiliary shape/distribution terms can change QRS/ST preservation and waveform fidelity, while frozen-classifier AUROC need not move in the same direction. No cell wins every endpoint, and post hoc maxima are exploratory. Current authority resides in results/factorial_v4/ plus the generation registry and protocol audit; the removed comprehensive_latest_48_models path is not used.

title: 28  Smartwatch Simulator Transfer and Frozen-Classifier Fidelity
text:
28.1 Artifact and schema gate
This chapter reads the current factorial_v4_clinical artifacts directly. It separates two estimands: device/protocol measurement error against programmed simulator values or paired Philips recordings, and frozen-classifier probability fidelity between reference and reconstructed waveforms. Neither supplies human diagnostic ground truth. The task table records ground_truth_status = unavailable; clinical accuracy and interchangeability are not estimable here.

from pathlib import Path
import hashlib, json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display

ROOT = Path("..").resolve()
CLINICAL = ROOT / "results/factorial_v4_clinical"
PROTOCOL_CSV = CLINICAL / "smartwatch_protocol_metrics.csv"
FIDELITY_CSV = CLINICAL / "smartwatch_task_fidelity.csv"
COMPLETION_JSON = CLINICAL / "FINAL_COMPLETION.json"
MANIFEST_JSON = CLINICAL / "clinical_database_manifest.json"
required = [PROTOCOL_CSV, FIDELITY_CSV, COMPLETION_JSON, MANIFEST_JSON]
missing = [str(path) for path in required if not path.is_file()]
if missing:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"Required current smartwatch artifacts are missing: {missing}")

def sha256_file(path):
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as handle:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: handle.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
            digest.update(chunk)
    return digest.hexdigest()

protocol = pd.read_csv(PROTOCOL_CSV)
fidelity = pd.read_csv(FIDELITY_CSV)
completion = json.loads(COMPLETION_JSON.read_text())
manifest = json.loads(MANIFEST_JSON.read_text())
declared_paths = []
for value in manifest.values():
    if isinstance(value, str) and ("/" in value or value.endswith((".csv", ".parquet", ".db"))):
        p = Path(value)
        if not p.is_absolute(): p = ROOT / p
        declared_paths.append(p)
missing_declared = sorted(str(p.relative_to(ROOT)) for p in declared_paths if not p.exists())
expected_devices = {"applewatch_serie8", "fitbitsense2", "samsunggalaxy6", "withingsscanwatch"}
assert set(protocol.device) == expected_devices
assert set(fidelity.device) == expected_devices
assert fidelity.model_id.nunique() == 48
assert fidelity.task_name.nunique() == 150
assert fidelity[["model_id", "device", "task_name"]].duplicated().sum() == 0
assert len(fidelity) == 48 * 4 * 150
assert set(fidelity.ground_truth_status) == {"unavailable"}

title: 28  Smartwatch Simulator Transfer and Frozen-Classifier Fidelity
text:
28.5 Interpretation boundary
The artifacts show that reconstruction changes a frozen classifier’s probabilities and that change varies across tasks, devices, architectures, and objectives. Before a clinical transfer claim, the study still requires record-level outputs joined to independently adjudicated labels, patient-level identity and clustered uncertainty, prespecified primary tasks and multiplicity control, simple baselines, per-lead waveform endpoints, alignment sensitivity, protocol-stratified failure cases, and a passed independent post-run audit.
Reproduction sources are smartwatch_protocol_metrics.csv, smartwatch_task_fidelity.csv, clinical_database_manifest.json, and FINAL_COMPLETION.json under results/factorial_v4_clinical/. Rendering is read-only and generates no CSV.
